Akito Kawahara and colleagues built a family tree for hawkmoths in 2009 using five nuclear genes. Hawkmoths number about fourteen hundred species and serve as test cases across biology. Yet their family links, built mostly on body form, were shaky.

Gene data gave the team a firmer tree and a view of how the moths spread across the globe. A solid tree lets other work, from flight studies to pest control, rest on real kinship. The study replaces guesswork about hawkmoth history with evidence from the moths' own DNA. It covers one of the most watched moth families in science.
plos-pone-0005819:
Nishaki Mehta and co-authors made HIV testing cheaper in 2009 by validating diagnosis from dried blood spots. A spot of blood dried on paper is easy to collect, store, and ship where labs are scarce. Real-time PCR can then measure the virus from that spot.

Their method both detects HIV and counts its load at low cost. Early treatment of infected infants is now advised, which needs exactly this kind of test. The approach fits clinics that lack freezers, couriers, or big budgets. The team shows performance data to back its use in limited-resource settings.
plos-pone-0006419:
Steroid treatment can starve bone of blood until the bone dies, a condition called osteonecrosis. Ge Zhang and colleagues tested flavonoids from the herb Epimedium in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Two events interrupt bone blood supply: clotting inside vessels and fat deposits outside them. No clinical agent targets both at once.

The Epimedium flavonoids reduced the incidence of steroid-associated osteonecrosis in a dose-dependent way. The effect did not come via direct action on the expected cellular targets, the title notes. The compounds may act through circulation rather than bone cells. A plant-derived candidate for an untreatable side effect deserves the attention.
plos-pone-0006519:
Hridayesh Prakash and co-authors studied a protein that helps infected lung cells stay alive, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The germ Chlamydophila pneumoniae infects the lung and lives inside its cells. Cells it infects resist apoptosis, the built-in death program of cells. That stand has been tied to a protein called cIAP-1, which blocks cell death.

The team asked how cIAP-1 shapes the first immune response to this lung germ. A germ that keeps its host cell alive gains a safe home. If that shield could be lifted, the body might clear the germ more fast. The work shows the push and pull between the germ and the cell it lives in.
plos-pone-0006619:
Isabel Calvo and co-authors ran a genome-wide screen for caffeine tolerance in fission yeast in PLOS ONE in 2009. An excess of caffeine is cytotoxic to all eukaryotic cell types. The team aim to study how cells become tolerant to a toxic dose of this drug. They also study the relationship between caffeine tolerance and other stresses.

A genome-wide screen of genes required for caffeine tolerance tests every gene for its contribution. Yeast screens are fast and complete, giving a parts list for drug defense. Many tolerance genes will have human counterparts. The work also illuminates how caffeine affects cells beyond its stimulant fame.
plos-pone-0009419:
Michael Hofreiter and co-authors published this ape diet study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bonobos and gorillas are hard to watch in dense forest. Their droppings, though, carry DNA that can betray what they ate. Earlier work had found vertebrate DNA in ape feces, which hinted at meat eating.

The team asked whether that DNA means real meat consumption or a lab artefact. They examined fecal samples from bonobos and gorillas for animal DNA. Sorting true diet from contamination matters because meat eating in apes bears on human evolution. The study tests how much trust to place in this detective method.
plos-pone-0009519:
Nicolas Maunoury and co-authors followed gene activity in root nodules in PLOS ONE in 2010. The plant Medicago truncatula hosts bacteria that turn air nitrogen into plant food. They meet in nodules, small organs on the roots. Inside, both plant cells and bacteria change into working partners. The team tracked gene switches across that change.

They found two big switch points in gene activity. Those switches keep plant cell growth and bacterial change in step. The picture shows how a partnership is choreographed at the gene level. Understanding it could help bring nitrogen fixing to more crops, cutting the need for fertilizer.
plos-pone-0009619:
Anna Divoli, Michael Wooldridge, and Marti Hearst tested a new way to search science papers in PLOS ONE in 2010. Biologists often judge a paper by its figures and captions. Standard search tools index mainly words in the text. The team built BioText, a search engine that also indexes full text with figures. They asked users to try real search tasks with each approach.

Showing full text and figures improved how well people found what they needed. Readers could judge relevance at a glance from images. The study gives evidence for a simple idea: search should match how scientists actually read. It points to richer displays as more than a cosmetic upgrade.
plos-pone-0010419:
Laura Morelli and colleagues compared Y-chromosome data from Sardinia and Anatolia in PLOS ONE in 2010. Farming spread across Europe in the Neolithic age, transforming life. Two stories explain how: farmers themselves moved in, or local hunters adopted the new ways. The stories are called demic and cultural diffusion. Male-line DNA can help tell them apart, since it tracks men's movements.

Patterns in the two regions fit cultural spread better than mass migration. That suggests ideas traveled more than whole peoples did, at least on these routes. Sardinians and Anatolians thus inform a Europe-wide debate. Genes, here, act as travel records for ancient men. The verdict favors teaching and trade over invasion as farming's engine.
plos-pone-0010519:
Thomas Hofmann and colleagues showed a channel protein is vital for controlling magnesium in fruit flies in PLOS ONE in 2010. Channels in the TRPM family do many jobs, from sensing to mineral balance. Most animals carry several members of this family; humans have eight. Flies are odd: they carry essentially one. That made the fly a clean test of what that single channel does.

Removing it disrupted the flies' control of magnesium outside their cells. Magnesium is a mineral every cell needs in tight amounts. A single-channel animal shows the channel's core job without backup systems hiding it. The work may clarify human mineral disorders linked to related channels. Simplicity, here, is the experiment's strength.
plos-pone-0010619:
Bo Hu and colleagues built a small artificial ecosystem in PLOS ONE in 2010. Natural microbe communities are too tangled to study piece by piece. The team instead assembled a simple synthetic community whose members react to their surroundings.

Each microbe strain played a defined role in the group. When conditions changed, the whole community shifted its behavior in response. That made the system a clean and useful test bed for basic ecology questions. Controlled communities like this could also serve industry, where mixed microbes already make fuels and chemicals. Its members were chosen, not found.
plos-pone-0010719:
Takashi Irie and colleagues dissected how Sendai virus dodges early immune defenses, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sendai virus infects mice and is a close model for human respiratory viruses. Its C protein works at several steps of infection and blunts the interferon warning system.

A small set of charged building blocks in the C protein did much of that work. Changing them weakened the virus's ability to hide in cells and in mice. One protein thus juggles several tricks with the same toolkit. Mapping the toolkit shows where a weakened virus for vaccine study could be made more safely.
plos-pone-0010819:
Qian Wu and colleagues linked failed cell division to cancer signaling, in PLOS ONE in 2010. When a cell divides its body but fails to split in two, it ends with double chromosomes. Such cells appear in early cancers. A platelet protein called glycoprotein 1b alpha, targeted by the cancer gene c-Myc, was the team's focus in cultured human cells.

The protein connected division failure to known cancer-driving pathways. Cells with division errors switched those pathways on through it. A mechanical accident thus becomes a chemical growth signal. The link helps explain why chromosome-doubled cells so often turn malignant, and it names a protein where the chain might be cut.
plos-pone-0010919:
Glen Spraggon, Eric Koesema, Maria Scarselli and co-authors published this structural biology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Streptococcus pneumoniae, a major cause of pneumonia and meningitis, grips host cells with hair-like pili built from repeating protein units. The team reconstructed how the backbone protein, RrgB, locks together in those chains.

They combined electron microscope images of pilus pieces with an atomic crystal structure of most of RrgB, then fitted the two together. The fit shows neighboring units arranged in a single defined pattern, rather than a loose tangle. Spraggon and colleagues give the first clear picture of how this bacterial grappling hook is assembled. Such blueprints help vaccine designers, since pilus proteins are promising targets for preventing pneumococcal disease.
plos-pone-0011019:
Carla Palma, Silvia Vendetti and Antonio Cassone published this tuberculosis immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The CD4 T cells that secrete interferon-gamma protect against TB, yet uncontrolled amounts of the same response damage lungs and spoil vaccine protection. The authors found, in mice, a natural brake on that response operated by a different T cell class.

Two vaccination regimens against a TB antigen produced either a modest, protective response or a massive, non-protective one, and both generated CD8 T cells that suppressed the CD4 cells' interferon output. The receptor 4-1BB on those CD8 cells was central to their controlling role. Palma and colleagues identify a built-in thermostat for vaccine responses. Harnessing it could help TB vaccines stay protective instead of tipping into harm.
plos-pone-0011119:
Nakamura, Kinoshita, Yokoi and colleagues proposed a new cause of dry eye in PLOS ONE in 2010. People who work at screens all day often report dry, sore eyes. Blinking drops during screen use, but the authors pointed to another factor: weak tear glands.

They argued that the tear making glands underperform in many screen users, a state they call lacrimal hypofunction. Naming this mechanism widens dry eye care beyond drops and blink breaks. Treatments that restore gland function could help a growing group of patients. The study links a modern work habit to a specific, testable fault in the eye.
plos-pone-0011219:
Chambrion and Le Naour studied cell surface proteins in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells crawl using groups of surface proteins that work together. Two of these proteins, from the tetraspanin family, were tested for how they control the effects of a partner protein on cell migration.

Both proteins regulated how strongly the partner drove cells to move. That circuit matters because uncontrolled migration lets cancers spread through the body. A control circuit offers points where movement might be restrained by drugs. The finding informs metastasis research with specific, named members of the circuit.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1219:
The Secretary of State wrote to Ambassador Hurley in China on 28 July 1945. Outgoing word from the secretary set the line for the China post. It went out in the summit's last week, while the secretary's own days were filled with the German talks.

A secretary's cable to an envoy joins two files at once: the sender's talks and the reader's post. Hurley needed the summit's drift to do his work in China. This message supplied the chief's word straight from Potsdam. It is the return half of the Hurley channel, matching the ambassador's own reports printed nearby.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1319:
Pauley wrote to the Secretary of State on 20 July 1945. His reparations reports went to both the president and the chief envoy that week. The commission's work in Moscow and Germany fed straight into the summit's central money fight.

What Germany would pay, in what form, and from which zones were the questions Pauley's facts had to answer. His note to Byrnes put that evidence in the negotiator's own hands. This message is the reparations thread at the working level of the talks. It shows the expert and the bargainer joined, one day into the hardest part of the summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1419:
A second memorandum by Charles Bohlen, also dated 28 March 1960, accompanies the Yalta texts at the back of the Potsdam volume. Bohlen knew the Soviet leaders and their language as few Americans did. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Two memoranda from the same day by the same hand suggest a man clearing his desk of a subject that would not leave him. Yalta had become a political charge in America by 1960, blamed by some for the cold war itself. Bohlen, who had taken notes and translated at the talks, answered from memory and record. His pair of papers closes the volume on a note of reflection rather than decision.
frus-1945-50-intel-d19:
Hoover wrote to Attorney General Clark on 27 September 1945, a week after the OSS order. The FBI director kept up a steady flow of paper to his chief through the autumn. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The dissolution of the OSS opened ground that Hoover meant the FBI to hold, above all in the Western Hemisphere. His letters after the order pressed the bureau's advantage while rivals regrouped. Readers can track a pattern across the Hoover papers: each one restates the bureau's claim in fresh terms for a fresh moment. This letter belongs to the first week of the new order of things, when the map of American intelligence lay open.
frus-1945-50-intel-d119:
A draft letter from President Truman to Attorney General Clark is dated 7 August 1946. Drafts prepared for a president's signature show a decision being readied at the top. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The FBI answered to the attorney general, so a presidential letter to Clark was the heaviest paper that could enter the Latin American fight. That it survives as a draft is itself part of the story: drafts are where decisions can still be softened, delayed, or dropped. Readers should compare the draft with the authority's letter to Clark sent the next day. The two papers together show the White House and the board dividing the work of settling the dispute.
frus-1945-50-intel-d219: "Central Intelligence Group Memorandum" bears the date 21 July 1947. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 219 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The bill that would create the CIA was in its last stages in Congress, and offices across Washington were getting ready. Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next.
frus-1945-50-intel-d319:
Minutes record the 10th Meeting of the National Intelligence Authority on 26 June 1947. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 319, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Congress was then debating the National Security Act, the law that would soon create the CIA and the National Security Council.

As minutes, the text sticks to the business of the meeting: items raised, views stated in brief, and the choices the group reached. They rarely give long speeches, but they fix the choices that later memos then carry out. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d419:
W. Park Armstrong sent a memo to Under Secretary of State James Webb on 6 March 1950. It is document 419 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950, one of several Armstrong papers in the file.

Armstrong headed the State Department's research and intelligence office under Secretary Dean Acheson. His memos to Webb brought the analysts' voice into the room where the department was run. Read with his other papers, this one shows a bureau chief pressing his office's worth, week after week. The March date places the memo in a season of fresh debate over the agency's future shape.
frus-1861-d19:
On 21 October 1861, William H. Seward directed a fresh letter to Norman Judd in Berlin. The dispatch is document 19 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Late October 1861 found Seward juggling crises on many fronts at once. His letters to Berlin formed one thread of a much wider web. In this one he directs his minister in Prussia, keeping the northern German court inside the Union's steady campaign against foreign aid to the South. The letter reached Berlin as the leaves fell, into a court deep in its own affairs. His brief from Washington was the same that month as in the spring: hold fast.
frus-1861-d119:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William Dayton on 22 April 1861. Dayton was the new American minister to France, based in Paris. The letter is document 119 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Paris stood second only to London in the war's foreign stakes. The Emperor Napoleon III watched for a chance to favor the South. Seward's April letter set Dayton, a former senator, to guard that gate from the war's first days. Dayton had run for Vice President in 1856, which gave him rank in Paris talk. Rank in Paris talk opened doors that a plain envoy would have found barred.
frus-1861-d219:
Another report crossed the ocean to Seward, this one from Mr. Marsh on 2 September 1861. It stands as Document 219 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. The letter comes from the first summer of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d19:
The home office spoke to Charles Francis Adams on 14 February 1862, through a letter from Seward. It stands as Document 19 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. By then, in the winter of the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d119:
On 4 August 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as Document 119 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. By then, in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d219:
From Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent William Stuart a letter on 24 June 1862, printed as Document 219 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart led the British legation in Washington while Lord Lyons was absent that year.

Three letters in five days show the pace Seward set when business pressed. The matters at hand in such notes were often narrow: a seized ship, a detained man, a point of form. Yet each small case, handled badly, could feed the larger quarrel over Britain's part in the war. The Stuart letters repay reading as a set. Britain's first concern in Washington was the blockade and what it cost British trade.
frus-1862-d319:
A Dayton report dated 8 August 1862 stands out of order as Document 319 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

This report duplicates the date of Document 301, and the pair shows how the legation's output could scatter in the printed volume. Both letters belong to the week Cedar Mountain was fought in Virginia. For the reader, matching the two restores the Paris post's full account of that week in the summer of 1862. Edouard Thouvenel ran the French foreign ministry for most of 1862 and set Dayton's agenda there.
frus-1862-d419:
Horace J. Perry sent this report from Madrid to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 3 May 1862. It is Document 419 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

In May 1862 the fall of New Orleans strengthened the Union's hand abroad, and agents like Perry used such news at court. Spain's stake was direct: Cuba's trade, the Gulf blockade, and the unraveling allied campaign in Mexico. A report from Madrid told Washington whether Spanish ministers leaned toward the Union, the Confederacy, or simple caution. Perry's letters are the raw feed behind Seward's answers to Madrid that season.
frus-1862-d519:
James Shepherd Pike reported from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 17 September 1862, the day of Antietam in far-off Maryland. The dispatch is Document 519 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Pike could know nothing of the battle as he wrote; his letter reflects the Netherlands as it stood on Dutch news alone. That innocence is part of the record's value. It shows what a friendly small power thought of the war at the very hinge of its fortunes. Victory claims and the emancipation order had not yet reset every calculation. Seward read the letter weeks later, in a changed world, as one more fixed point in his map of European opinion.
frus-1862-d619:
Bradford R. Wood, the American minister at Copenhagen, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 4 November 1862. It is Document 619 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the Danish file's only printed report.

Wood's November letter gave Washington the Danish reading of the war in its second autumn. It covered the court's temper and the press. It also covered the maritime business between the two countries. A single report in a file of instructions is itself informative; Copenhagen needed little reporting because little there was in doubt. The dispatch completes the small Danish record for 1862. The record is a study in what much of the Union's diplomacy really was. It was the steady care of friendly, uncomplicated relationships.
frus-1862-d719:
Friedrich Hassaurek wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 2 October 1862. Hassaurek was the American minister in Ecuador, a German-born Ohio lawyer and writer. The letter is document 719 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Ecuador sat far down the Pacific coast, and its envoy's mail reached Washington slowly. Hassaurek reported on the land's politics and on the trade of its ports, where American ships called for goods. His letters were the State Department's main word from that coast. This dispatch is part of that thin but steady line, kept up by one man writing from Quito while his country fought at home.
frus-1863p1-d19:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 24 December 1862. Adams was the American minister in London, writing on Christmas Eve. The letter is document 19 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

A holiday date did not slow the legation's mail. Adams wrote through the season on the state of British feeling and the work of the South's friends in Europe. His calm, exact tone is part of why his file still reads well. This dispatch is a late-year piece of the London watch. It was sent while Washington waited for word of the new year and the freedom edict soon to come.
frus-1863p1-d119:
On 16 March 1863, William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the first of four letters to him dated that day in the volume. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 119 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Four sheets in a day is another desk-clearing, smaller than the dozen of 2 March but of the same kind. Seward took the London file head by head, one point per page. This letter opens the set. The batch habit shows how the brief was run. It ran not by long essays, but by short, sharp notes an envoy could act on one at a time.
frus-1863p1-d219:
From his London post on 19 June 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 219 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Public meetings across Britain, many of them backing the Union and emancipation, formed part of the picture Adams reported. He tracked opinion as carefully as he tracked ministers. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d319:
To Mr. Stuart of the British legation in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote on 11 November 1862. The note is document 319 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Stuart served at the British legation in Washington and handled business with the State Department when the minister himself was away or occupied. His notes form part of the same Anglo-American exchange. It comes from the autumn after Antietam, when Lincoln's first emancipation order had just raised the stakes for Britain. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d419:
The American answer to London on 20 March 1863 took the form of this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 419 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

The two men met and wrote constantly, and both knew a quarrel between their countries could hand the South its independence. That shared fear kept the tone correct even when the words were sharp. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d519:
One entry in the 1863 papers is a 18 May 1863 letter from Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid.
frus-1863p1-d619:
A dispatch dated 15 September 1863 went from William H. Seward, the Secretary of State to Britain's chargé d'affaires William Stuart. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
plos-pbio-0020219:
Konstantinos Zarbalis, Scott R. May, Yiguo Shen, and co-workers set out a mouse screening strategy in PLOS Biology in 2004. Random mutations can reveal genes that build the brain's cortex, the wrinkled outer layer where thought happens. Screening every mutant mouse the old way is slow and costly.

Their focused plan checks likely mutants first and uses clear signs to pick the ones worth deep study. With it, they found mutations that disrupt cortex development. Each such mutant is a clue to how the cortex is wired as it grows. A sharper screen speeds the whole field, since good mouse models of brain disorders are prized and hard to make.
plos-pone-0000119:
Fabrizio Gelain, Daniele Bottai, Angleo Vescovi, and colleagues published this tissue engineering paper in PLOS ONE in 2006. They built designer scaffolds from self-assembling peptides, tiny protein pieces that line up into nanofibers on their own. The scaffolds were used to grow adult mouse neural stem cells in three dimensions.

Growing brain stem cells in 3-D, rather than flat on a dish, better mimics real tissue. The authors describe how the cells take to these tailor-made fiber networks. The approach points toward lab-grown material that could one day support nerve repair. It also gives stem cell researchers a tunable tool for testing growth conditions.
plos-pone-0000219:
Noah Fahlgren, Miya D. Howell, Kristin D. Kasschau, and colleagues published this plant genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Using high-throughput sequencing, the team catalogued microRNAs in Arabidopsis, the model plant. Their evidence points to frequent birth and death of MIRNA genes, the genes that make these tiny regulators.

MicroRNA genes turn over fast, appearing and vanishing across generations of plants. Documenting that churn in a single well-studied species shows how regulation evolves. The sequencing data also expanded the known set of Arabidopsis microRNAs, a resource other plant biologists build on.
plos-pone-0000319:
Victor M. Rodriguez-Molina, Ad Aertsen, and Detlef H. Heck published this neuroscience theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cortical pyramidal neurons are the main output cells of the cortex, and their spike timing, the exact moments they fire, may carry information. The authors model how EPSC kinetics, input synchronization, and background noise affect the reliability of that timing.

Precise firing matters if the brain uses time as a code. The model weighs three influences that sharpen or blur a neuron's timing. The results help interpret recordings from real cortex, where all three influences are always present together.
plos-pone-0000419:
Baochuan Lin and colleagues applied a broad pathogen-hunting method to samples from a city population, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Most tests look for one germ at a time. Their approach is sequence-based and broad-spectrum: it reads genetic material to identify many possible pathogens at once, including ones nobody suspected.

A test that names whatever is there could catch outbreaks earlier and solve infections that single tests miss. Applying it in an urban population checks whether the method survives real-world messiness. The work points toward surveillance systems that watch for the unexpected, not only for the diseases already on a checklist.
plos-pone-0000519:
Susan Marino and Roel Nusse reported mouse mutants that reveal a chromatin machine's importance before birth, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The mutants disable P66α, a component of the NuRD/Mi2 complex, which remodels chromatin, the packaging of DNA, to control genes. The title states the outcome plainly: the mutants are embryonic lethal.

Embryonic lethality means the complex is not optional equipment; development fails without it. Such all-or-nothing results tell biologists which regulators sit at the center of the gene-control web. They also set the stage for finer experiments that disable the protein in one tissue or stage at a time.
plos-pone-0000619:
Miriam Zacksenhouse, Mikhail A. Lebedev, Jose M. Carmena and co-authors tracked brain signals in early brain-machine interface sessions for PLOS ONE in 2007. Such interfaces read activity from motor cortex neurons and use it to drive artificial devices. When a person plans or makes a reaching movement, those neurons change their firing in many ways at once.

The team reports that cortical modulations grow during the first sessions with the interface. In plain terms, the brain's signal patterns become stronger as practice begins. That growth matters for anyone building devices controlled by thought, because the interface and the brain adapt to each other from the very start.
plos-pone-0000719:
Lan Lan Liang Yeh, Jah-Yao Liu, Kao-Si Lin and colleagues put an 800-year-old herbal formula through a modern trial, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Most traditional Chinese formulas combine at least four herbs. Four-Agents-Decoction, or Si Wu Tang, contains four herbs and has long been used in Taiwan to relieve menstrual discomfort. No specific effect, however, had been established by controlled testing.

Their trial was randomised and placebo-controlled, the design that separates real effects from expectation. The condition was primary dysmenorrhoea, painful periods without an underlying disease. Old remedies deserve fair tests rather than dismissal or blind trust. A rigorous trial gives women and doctors evidence either way.
plos-pone-0000819:
Jürgen Glas, Julia Seiderer, Martin Wetzke and colleagues tested a bowel disease gene variant in a large German patient group, for PLOS ONE in 2007. The IL23R gene had been identified as a susceptibility gene for inflammatory bowel disease in the North American population. Their aim was to test that association in German Crohn's disease patients, and to look for interactions with other IBD genes.

The combined analysis covered IL23R, CARD15, and OCTN1/2 variants. The title names their headline result: variant rs1004819 is the main disease-associated IL23R variant in German patients. Replication in a second population matters, because genetic associations that travel across populations are likelier to be real and useful.
plos-pone-0000919:
Orest Szczurko, Kieran Cooley, Jason Busse and colleagues ran a randomized trial of naturopathic care for chronic low back pain, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Long lasting back pain costs employers heavily in health coverage and lost work days. Many patients try naturopathic care, a mix of diet advice, exercise and natural treatments, but hard trial evidence was thin.

The team randomized seventy-five postal workers to test whether the care helped. A randomized design, where chance assigns the treatment, is the fairest way to judge. Whatever the outcome, trials like this move a popular therapy out of the realm of claims. They give patients and insurers results they can weigh.
plos-pone-0001019:
Aaron Filler traced how body segment patterns diversified across mammals, in a solo PLOS ONE article from 2007. Homeotic genes set the identity of body segments, yet little was known about how their traits evolved over the mammal radiation. The spine is one place those patterns show plainly.

Filler reports an array of homeotic gradients that appear and diversify across mammal groups, generating new body plans. The work extends to the morphogenetic basis of human origins, how our own segment pattern arose. Reading mammal diversity as variations on shared gradients gives anatomy a developmental logic. It also explains odd spine counts that once looked like noise.
plos-pone-0001119:
Medical scans show the brain and skull as flat pictures, even though both are complex three-dimensional shapes. Daniel Kelley and co-authors describe a way around that limit in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They turn scan data into solid physical models using stereolithography, a form of 3D printing.

The team developed and validated a method for building accurate models of the brain and skull from medical images. A solid model can be held, turned, and studied from any angle, which flat images do not allow. Such models can support teaching, surgical planning, and a clearer grasp of how the structures fit together.
plos-pone-0001219:
Electrical signals from muscles, called EMG signals, let people control prostheses and computers by tensing a muscle. Eric Fimbel and Martin Arguin studied how well older people manage that control, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. An earlier experiment with young participants was replicated with elderly persons.

The authors assessed the effect of age on myocontrol, the ability to steer devices through muscle signals. Assistive technology is aimed largely at older users, so performance in the young is the wrong benchmark. Their results inform how such interfaces should be designed and calibrated for the people who actually need them.
plos-pone-0001319:
Insects smell their world through families of chemoreceptor proteins, but almost nothing was known about those receptors in beetles. Mohatmed Abdel-latief described a family of chemoreceptors in the red flour beetle, Tribolium castaneum, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Chemoperception in invertebrates is mediated by G-protein-coupled receptors.

The beetle's genome had recently been sequenced, making it a model species for beetle biology. The authors catalogued its chemoreceptor genes as a first step. Knowing a pest's smell receptors opens routes to traps and repellents that target its senses. The gene list gives that work a starting point.
plos-pone-0001419:
Vincent Béringue and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on variant CJD, the human form of mad cow disease. How wide the epidemic would grow was hard to call. Many who carry the agent may never show signs, or may show an odd form. The team used mice bred with the human gene to track infection.

In these mice, infection took hold far beyond the brain and stayed for a long time. That broad spread was both marked and lasting. It hints that silent carriers could hold the agent in many tissues. Such facts shape blood safety rules and the long watch kept on this disease.
plos-pone-0001519:
Marco Ajelli and Stefano Merler published a 2008 PLOS ONE model of flu spread between people. Models that track each person have grown key for pandemic plans. They count set contacts, such as home, school, and work ties. Loose, chance contacts are harder to count. The pair asked how much that loose part sways the outcome.

They found the loose contact share can shift both spread pace and the worth of control steps. Leaving it out can bias a model's verdict. Pandemic teams should thus test a range of loose contact rates. The work is a check on the tools that guide real world plans.
plos-pone-0001619:
Alicia Fajardo and her co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE research article about a hard problem in medicine. Some germs are born able to resist antibiotics. Doctors call the full set of these built-in defenses the intrinsic resistome. Most experts had blamed two causes, cell walls that drugs cannot cross and pumps that push drugs back out of the cell.

Fajardo's team tested that view by studying transposon mutants, germs with single genes knocked out at random. Their work points to a wider set of genes behind built-in drug resistance than the usual two causes suggest. The full text sets out the mutant screen and the genes it flagged. It also shows why a fuller map of these defenses could guide the search for drugs that still work.
plos-pone-0001719:
Wenbin Ye and co-authors studied the fine shape of the bond between microRNAs and their targets in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. MicroRNAs guide the repression of messenger RNAs after they are made. Hundreds are known, but finding which mRNAs each one targets in mammals is hard, partly because the pairing rules are poorly understood.

The team focused on central loops, bulges in the middle of the miRNA to target duplex, and measured how they affect repression efficiency. The full text gives the pairings tested and the gene regulation readouts. Sharper pairing rules mean better computer predictions of microRNA targets, a step needed before these tiny regulators can be fully mapped or used as drugs.
plos-pone-0001819:
Paula H. A. Ronkainen, Eija Pöllänen, Timo Törmäkangas, and their co-authors studied a gene affecting muscle in older women in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Muscle strength declines on average by one percent a year from midlife. In postmenopausal women that decline coincides with a rapid drop in estrogen production. The genetics behind estrogen's effects on skeletal muscle remained unclear.

The team reports that a polymorphism in the COMT gene is associated with skeletal muscle properties in older women. The gene's full name is catechol-O-methyltransferase, and the effect appears alone and together with physical activity. The full text gives the muscle tests and the gene comparisons. Gene-activity interactions like this point toward exercise prescriptions tuned to a woman's genetic profile.
plos-pone-0001919:
Svetlana Novikova and co-authors studied what cocaine use in pregnancy does to the brains of mouse pups, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Past work had shown clear changes in how the young of cocaine-exposed mothers behave. The team tested a deeper idea: that the drug warps the fetal system that tags DNA, leaving lasting marks on brain chemistry.

They gave cocaine to pregnant mice and then checked pups at birth and before puberty. The focus was the hippocampus, a brain area for memory, where they measured DNA methylation and which genes were switched on. Lasting tags there could help explain why early drug exposure shapes later acts.
plos-pone-0002019:
Glen Duncan and co-authors used twins to sort genes from surroundings in exercise habits, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Regular physical activity is well known to protect health. Yet how much of a person's activity level is inherited, and how much comes from their setting, was still disputed. The team set a cut point of sixty minutes of total activity per week.

Twin data let them split the effects of shared genes, shared home life, and each person's unique setting. As the title stresses, unique environmental effects stand out in who takes part. If settings drive activity more than genes, changes to daily life may move people more than advice alone.
plos-pone-0002119:
Martina Proell and co-authors published a review in PLOS ONE in 2008. Its subject is the Nod-like receptor family, a group of proteins often shortened to NLRs. These proteins sit inside cells and help the innate immune system, the body's fast first line of defense, sense signs of infection and damage.

The review sets out what the family members share and where they differ. It covers how NLRs are grouped, how they are thought to switch on immune responses, and why they sit at the core of many diseases. Readers get a clear map of a protein family that was then drawing fast-growing interest in immune research.
plos-pone-0002219:
Alexandre Zenon, Suliann Ben Hamed, and Jean-René Duhamel tracked the focus of attention during hard visual searches, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Spotting prey or a predator depends on pulling the right sight out of a busy scene fast. In the lab, visual search tasks copy that challenge: a subject must find one target among many distractors.

When the target is hard to tell apart, the search is slow and attention must be guided step by step. The team mapped how that guidance unfolds in space and time. Their results show the order in which the brain checks each part of a cluttered scene while hunting for a hard target.
plos-pone-0002319:
Flonia Levy-Adam and co-authors found a second job for an enzyme that chews up a common cell coating, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Heparanase cuts heparan sulfate, a sugar chain found on cell surfaces and in the matrix between cells. Its cutting helps tissues remodel and lets cancer cells spread.

The team reports that heparanase also works without cutting: it helps cells adhere and spread by clustering the heparan sulfate proteoglycans on the cell surface. Bringing those surface molecules together can fire growth signals. A non-cutting role matters for drug design, since blocking the enzyme's blade may not block this second activity.
plos-pone-0002419:
Prins led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Kurt W. Prins, Dawn A. Lowe, James M. Ervasti, among others. Its subject is skeletal Muscle-Specific Ablation of γ cyto -Actin Does Not Exacerbate the mdx Phenotype. We before documented a ten-fold increase in γ cyto -actin expression in dystrophin-deficient skeletal muscle.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002519:
Kondilis and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Barbara K. Kondilis, Ismene J. Kiriaze, Anastasia P. Athanasoulia, among others. Its subject is mapping Health Literacy Research in the European Union: A Bibliometric Analysis. To examine and compare the research productivity on selected fields related to health literacy of the current members of the European Union.

A bibliometric analysis (1991–2005). The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002619:
Betina Højgaard and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on waist circumference and body mass index as predictors of health care costs. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Betina Højgaard, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. In the present study we analyze the relationship between body mass index (BMI) and waist circumference (WC) and future health care costs. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002719:
A 2008 study by Zhan Gao and colleagues in PLOS ONE takes up substantial alterations of the cutaneous bacterial biota in psoriatic lesions. The catalog record names Zhan Gao first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. For psoriasis, an idiopathic inflammatory disorder of the skin, the microbial biota has not been defined using cultivation-independent methods. It goes on to note a further point. We used broad-range 16S rDNA PCR for archaea and bacteria to examine the microbiota of normal and psoriatic skin. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002819:
Arjan B. Brenkman and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on mdm2 induces Mono-Ubiquitination of FOXO4. Authorship is credited in the record to Arjan B. Brenkman and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The Forkhead box O (FOXO) class of transcription factors are involved in the regulation of several cellular responses including cell cycle progression and apoptosis. It goes on to note a further point. Furthermore, in model organisms FOXOs act as tumor suppressors and affect aging. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002919:
Arach Goldar, Hélène Labit, Kathrin Marheineke and co-authors modeled DNA copying in early embryos in 2008. Cells seem unable to check that copying is finished during a normal S phase, yet they must finish on time. In early Xenopus frog embryos the problem is sharp, since copy start sites switch on at random.

Their dynamic stochastic model treats start site firing as a chance process and works out how reliable finishing still results. Stochastic here means driven by random timing. Published in PLOS ONE, the model helps explain how embryos copy a whole genome fast without a central checker.
plos-pone-0003019:
Harald Staiger, Fausto Machicao, Konstantinos Kantartzis and co-authors tested new type 2 diabetes risk loci against prediabetic traits in 2008. Genome-wide studies had found a series of new risk loci, most later shown to affect insulin secretion by pancreatic beta cells. A fresh meta-analysis had just revealed nine more loci with unknown roles.

The title reports those new loci do not determine prediabetic phenotypes. In other words, carriers did not show the expected early traits. Published in PLOS ONE, the gap between genetic risk and measurable early signs is itself informative for screening ideas. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003119:
Masashi Fujihara, Norihiro Nagai, Thomas E. Sussan and co-authors published this mouse study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It asks whether long-term cigarette smoke can harm the retina in ways that look like early age-related macular degeneration, a common cause of vision loss in older adults. Two-month-old mice breathed either clean air or smoke in a chamber for five hours a day, five days a week.

The title reports the main result: smoke caused oxidative damage and cell death in the retinal pigmented epithelial cells, the layer that supports the light-sensing retina. Readers get a clear test of how smoke exposure links to eye damage, and why smoking may raise the risk of this eye disease.
plos-pone-0003219:
Yong Luo, Mauricio Alvarez, Lingchuan Xia and colleagues ask what happens to microbes when their host cell divides in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Macrophages can multiply, and certain microbes survive inside phagocytic cells. That raises the question of where the microbe cargo goes after the host cell splits. Using macrophage-like cells, the team checked how Cryptococcus yeast inside the cells is shared out after division.

The title reports that the outcome of phagocytic cell division with infectious cargo depends on single phagosome formation. Readers see lasting infection as a problem of cell division. If microbes cluster in one compartment, daughter cells may inherit them unevenly.
plos-pone-0003319:
Max-Philipp Stenner, Anne Waschbisch, Dorothea Buck and colleagues study a multiple sclerosis drug's effect on regulatory cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Natalizumab is a monoclonal humanized antibody targeting the alpha-4 chain of very late activation antigen 4. It has strong healing effects in patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. The goal was to study impacts of natalizumab therapy on Foxp3+ T regulatory cells.

Readers learn how a strong drug that blocks cell traffic affects the cells that calm immunity. That balance matters because blocking cell movement helps the brain but can raise infection risk. Tracking regulatory cells adds a safety layer and shows more of how the drug works.
plos-pone-0007419:
Ole Hartvig Mortensen, Anders Rinnov Nielsen, Christian Erikstrup, and colleagues proposed an inflammation protein as an obesity marker in 2009. Two inflammatory molecules, S100A8 and S100A9, form a combined protein called calprotectin. Plasma calprotectin levels are elevated in various inflammatory disorders, from arthritis to inflammatory bowel disease in clinical practice.

The authors hypothesize levels would rise in low-grade systemic inflammation as well. That state accompanies obesity. They test calprotectin as a novel marker of obesity. Their PLOS ONE paper evaluates whether a simple blood measure can capture the hidden inflammation that links obesity to disease.
plos-pone-0007519:
Lars Schwabe and Oliver Wolf published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the fragility of personal memories. A new memory starts out labile, then settles into stable storage. Recalling a settled memory makes it fragile again until it re-stabilizes, a step called reconsolidation. The team asked whether learning something new during that window interferes. Their test used autobiographical memories, the stories of a person's own life.

Fresh episodic learning did interfere with the reconsolidation of the recalled personal memories. The old memories came back altered by what was learned in between. That finding carries real stakes for therapy and for eyewitness accounts. It shows that remembering is not replaying a fixed record. Each recall opens a brief chance for the record to be edited, for better or worse.
plos-pone-0007619:
John Lukens and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the liver's unusual immune character. The liver is constantly exposed to bacterial products and food antigens from the gut. To avoid constant inflammation, it leans toward tolerance. The mediators that shape immune responses in that environment were not fully known. The team tested whether the liver itself can activate naive killer T cells in mice.

The liver can activate those CD8 T cells. The cells it produces, though, show dysfunctional antiviral activity. That is the tolerance trade-off made visible: response without full fighting power. Such a compromise protects the organ from friendly fire. It may also explain why some viruses persist in the liver. The study pinpoints the liver as an active teacher of T cells, not a passive bystander.
plos-pone-0007719:
Masaaki Adachi and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It looks at what happens when cells face heat and oxidative stress at once. Pollution and ozone loss raise oxidative stress, while warming raises heat exposure. People now risk meeting both at the same time.

Cells defend themselves with a heat stress response that rescues folded proteins. The authors found that oxidative stress weakens that defense. It also slows the recovery of proteins after heat damage. The result helps explain why combined stresses can harm health more than either one alone.
plos-pone-0007819:
David Gallego-Ortega and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It compares two sister enzymes that start a key fat-building path in human cells. Choline kinase is the first enzyme of the Kennedy pathway branch. That branch makes phosphocholine, a main part of cell membranes.

Humans carry two forms, alpha and beta, with different jobs. The authors map their differential roles in lipid metabolism. The split matters for cancer, where choline use runs high. It also matters for treatment, since blocking the wrong form could cause harm. The study guides which enzyme drug makers should target.
plos-pone-0007919:
Murugesan Rajaram and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It follows a dangerous bacterium's escape from the cell compartment meant to kill it. Francisella tularensis infects macrophages, the immune cells that eat germs. It breaks out of the phagosome and multiplies in the cell body.

Infected cells then die through the Fas-mediated death pathway. The authors show that pathway switches on as the bacterium escapes. Two cell proteins, Akt and SHIP, modulate the escape. The tug-of-war between germ and host decides the infection's course. Each control point is a possible therapy target.
plos-pone-0008019:
David Lambert and colleagues read DNA from museum skins of an extinct New Zealand bird in PLOS ONE in 2009. The huia was famed for its beak: the male's was short and stout, the female's long and curved, the widest such gap known in birds. The last birds died out a century ago.

Gene tests, sex checks, and careful measures of the old specimens let the team rebuild parts of the bird's family life and variety. Museum skins thus still speak. What they say can guide care for the huia's living kin and sharpen how we read other lost species.
plos-pone-0008119:
Aimee Shen and colleagues simplified protein cleaning with a tag that cuts itself off in PLOS ONE in 2009. Labs grow useful proteins in bacteria, then must fish them out pure. Tags help the fishing, but cutting the tag off usually adds steps and cost.

Their tag borrows a cutting enzyme from the cholera germ that snips only at one exact spot, its own joint. A trigger makes it cut on command, freeing the clean protein. Fewer steps mean less loss and fewer chances to spoil delicate proteins, a gain for labs large and small.
plos-pone-0008219:
Sean Myles and colleagues presented fast genome methods for grapes in a PLOS ONE paper from 2010. The genus Vitis includes the grapes used for wine and table fruit. New sequencing tools promise to speed the use of genetic data in crop improvement. Mapping genes for useful traits is a key step in breeding. Good study design comes before that mapping work.

The team showed how rapid genomic characterization can be done across the genus. A broad genetic picture helps breeders plan crosses and mapping studies. It can reveal diversity that breeding programs might otherwise miss. The work supports faster, smarter improvement of grape varieties.
plos-pone-0008319:
Carney D. Matheson and colleagues investigated an ancient tomb in Jerusalem in PLOS ONE in 2009. The Tomb of the Shroud dates to the first century of the common era. It was discovered in Akeldama, Jerusalem, and had been looted before study. An interdisciplinary team began investigating it in 2000. More than twenty stone ossuaries held human remains there.

Molecular methods were used to explore the tomb's contents. Ossuaries are boxes for collecting bones after burial. DNA and other traces can reveal kinship and disease among the dead. The work connects archaeology with laboratory science.
plos-pone-0008419:
Zhe Ji and Bin Tian studied messenger RNA endings in stem cells in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. The 3 prime untranslated regions of mRNAs contain elements that regulate gene expression after transcription. Over half of mammalian genes have multiple polyadenylation sites. Alternative choices produce different 3 prime regions for the same gene. The team examined this during generation of pluripotent stem cells.

Reprogramming cells from different types reshaped their mRNA endings. Shorter or longer tails change how messages are controlled. Such reprogramming may be part of how stem cells reset identity. The work links RNA processing to cell fate.
plos-pone-0008519:
Otto Erlwein and co-authors test a claimed virus link in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. In October 2009, a study reported a new retrovirus in chronic fatigue syndrome. The virus, called XMRV, had also been linked to prostate cancer. It was reported in most US patients in that study. If confirmed, the claim would reshape understanding of the syndrome. Erlwein's team try to detect XMRV in their own patient group.

They fail to detect the novel retrovirus in chronic fatigue cases. Their methods were able to find the virus if present at reported levels. A negative result of this kind tempers a high-profile claim. It shows why independent replication is essential in science.
plos-pone-0008619:
Khatira Anwari and co-authors describe a membrane machine in a germ in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Mitochondria, the power units of our cells, came from a free germ long ago. They still build their outer membrane much as that germ did. The germ studied here is Caulobacter crescentus, a model species. The team study its BAM complex. That machine inserts barrel-shaped proteins into the outer membrane.

They find the germ BAM complex is built from modules. Its modules echo the machine still used in mitochondria. Study of the germ version clarifies how mitochondria arose. It also reveals weak points in germ membranes that drugs could target.
plos-pone-0008719:
Soumyajit Banerjee Mustafi, Prabir Chakraborty, and Sanghamitra Raha traced how a grape compound attacks leukemia cells. Their work ran in PLOS ONE in 2010. Resveratrol is found in grape skins and red wine. It lowers levels of Hsp70, a protective protein, in chronic myelogenous leukemia cells. Lower Hsp70 helps push those cells to die. The route from compound to protein drop was unclear.

The team followed two signaling paths, Akt and ERK1/2, inside K562 leukemia cells. Resveratrol shifted both paths, and Hsp70 fell as a result. Mapping the route shows where similar drugs might strike leukemia cells.
plos-pone-0008819:
Koichi Matsumura, Maryanne Opiekun, Hiroaki Oka, and colleagues sniffed out lung cancer through urine odor. Their proof-of-principle study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lung cancer is the top cancer killer worldwide. It often grows silently until late stages. The body releases volatile compounds that change with disease. Breath studies had hinted such odor signatures exist.

Mouse models of lung cancer carried distinct urinary odor profiles. Trained detection could separate cancer urine from healthy urine. A urine test would be painless and cheap to repeat. Much work remains before human screening, but the principle held in mice.
plos-pone-0008919:
Martin Peifer, Jonathan Weiss, Martin Sos, and colleagues built a math method for judging drug pairs in fast cell screens. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Single cancer drugs often shrink tumors only briefly. Pairs of drugs can control tumors longer and better. Finding pairs that truly synergize, though, is slow. High-throughput screens test thousands of combinations on cells. Scoring synergy fairly across a whole population is the hard part.

Their lifetime modeling scores synergy from how cell populations fare over time. Population-level scoring resists the noise of single snapshots. Combination hunting for cancer drugs gets a sharper tool. Better pairs can reach animal testing sooner.
plos-pone-0009019:
Thomas Ray charted where psychedelic drugs attach across the whole human receptor set, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Psychedelics are thought to work mainly through two serotonin receptors, 5-HT2A and 5-HT2C. Drugs like the phenylalkylamines seem fairly choosy for those two. But a full census of their binding had not been assembled.

Ray mapped the drugs against the human receptorome, the full set of receptors. The chart shows which receptors each compound touches beyond the famous two. Some side targets may help explain differences between these drugs. A complete map warns against assuming one receptor explains the whole experience.
plos-pone-0009119:
Adriane Martin Hilber and co-authors pooled dozens of studies on vaginal practices and HIV risk, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many women use intravaginal practices to manage their health and sexual life. Cleansing the vagina and inserting substances are common in many regions. Such practices could harm the vaginal lining and invite infection, though.

The systematic review and meta-analysis asked two linked questions. Do these practices raise the rate of vaginal infections among women? And do they raise the chance of acquiring HIV during sex? Pooling the studies gives guidance that respects women's habits while cutting real risk.
plos-pone-0009219:
Santosh Kumar Patnaik, Eric Kannisto, and Sai Yendamuri published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA pieces that fine-tune how genes are used. Some microRNAs show up at odd levels in cancer tissue. Two of them, miR-30a and miR-191, had been flagged that way in lung samples.

The team forced lung cells to make extra amounts of each microRNA. They used a lung cancer line, A549, and a normal lung line, BEAS-2B. Despite the extra microRNA, the cells' behavior and appearance did not change. That negative result matters: a microRNA can mark cancer tissue without driving the cancer itself.
plos-pone-0009319:
Alain Dejean and co-authors published this ant survey in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tropical rainforest canopies are often ruled by a patchwork of dominant ant species. Each holds its own trees and fights off the others, forming an ant mosaic. The team checked whether such a mosaic exists on Madagascar's Masoala Peninsula.

They surveyed tree-dwelling ants along three transects set farther and farther from the coast. They mapped which dominant species held which areas and where gaps appeared. An invasive ant species was also present in the forest. The survey gives a baseline for a coastline where native and invader ants now meet.
plos-pone-0011419:
Lucy Parker and co-authors audited in 2010 the quality of studies that claim to diagnose disease from molecular fingerprints. Tests built on genomics and similar high-throughput methods promise much, but weak study design can make a test look far better than it is. A checklist tool called QUADOMICS was built to grade such studies, and the team put both the tool and recent papers to the test.

Their review of published diagnostic studies found common methodological holes, such as unclear patient selection and weak validation. The audit also judged how well the checklist itself catches those holes. The message is practical: journals and funders should require the checklist before a fingerprint test is celebrated. Patients are the ones harmed when a flawed test reaches the clinic, so quality control at the study stage is a form of patient protection.
plos-pone-0011519:
Rainer Lehmann and co-authors read the blood chemistry of exercising people in 2010 and found one molecule family in the lead. At a steady, moderate pace, the body shifts toward burning fat, and carrier molecules called acylcarnitines shuttle fat fuel into the cell's power stations. The team profiled these metabolites in people under moderate intensity exercise.

Medium-chain acylcarnitines dominated the metabolite pattern during exercise and supported continued lipid oxidation, the burning of fat. That lead pattern shows muscles switching fuel gears in an orderly way, not at random. The signature could serve as a marker of healthy fuel switching, which falters in diabetes and obesity. For fitness and metabolic medicine alike, the study turns the vague idea of fat burning into named molecules that rise on cue.
plos-pone-0011619:
Janine Quijano and co-authors studied gene signals that pattern the fruit fly wing, in PLOS ONE in 2010. One signal, called Wingless, helps lay out the wing as it grows. Another player, Sno, was already known to oppose a different growth signal in lab tests, but its true role in living animals was puzzling.

Working in developing fly wings, the team showed that Sno also pushes back against Wingless signalling. That opposition helps keep wing growth properly balanced. The finding adds a brake to a well-studied patterning system and may explain roles for the related genes in animal development more broadly.
plos-pone-0011719:
Victor Laguna-Torres and co-authors tracked respiratory viruses in Peru during the 2009 pandemic, in PLOS ONE in 2010. When the novel pandemic H1N1 influenza appeared, it entered a landscape already shared by other flu and flu-like viruses. The team sampled patients with influenza-like illness at health centres from January to July that year.

They describe how the mix of detected viruses changed before and after the pandemic strain arrived. The before-and-after picture shows the newcomer reshaping the viral landscape. Such tracking helps health systems anticipate which viruses will dominate once a pandemic strain takes hold.
plos-pone-0011819:
Alfredo Panebra and co-authors mapped how common gene patterns shape a drug-target receptor, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The beta-2 adrenergic receptor sits on many cell types, from airway muscle to heart cells. Drugs that act on it treat asthma, lung disease and heart failure, yet how well they work shifts a lot from person to person.

The team built common patterns, called haplotypes, from twenty-six variable sites in the receptor gene and tested how each pattern steers receptor levels and control. The map helps explain why one inhaler dose can help one patient and barely touch the next, a step toward dosing by genes.
plos-pone-0011919:
Roby Greenwald and co-workers searched in 2010 for a breath signal of severe asthma in children. Children with severe asthma often keep having symptoms despite treatment, and their airways show high levels of oxidative stress. Oddly, their airways hold too little of S-nitrosothiols, natural compounds that relax airway muscle.

The team found that formate in exhaled breath marks that shortage. A breath test is painless and repeatable, unlike sampling airway fluid directly. If the marker holds up, doctors could follow a hidden part of asthma chemistry during clinic visits and judge whether treatments restore what severe airways are missing.
plos-pone-0012019:
Christopher Turbill and Thomas Ruf argued in 2010 that aging shapes the lives of long-lived mammals far more than those of short-lived ones. Senescence, the decline with age, is widely detected in mammals, but its importance for fitness in wild populations was disputed. Evolutionary theory predicts decline begins when natural selection grows weak, which tracks adult survival rates.

By that logic, long-lived species spend a large share of life in the zone where aging bites, while short-lived ones mostly die young from other causes. The argument reframes aging from a lab curiosity into a major ecological force for elephants, whales, and humans alike. It also tells field biologists where to look hardest for aging's effects.
plos-pone-0012119:
Federica Briatore, Annarita Patrizi, Laura Viltono, and colleagues mapped calming synapses in the mouse cerebellum for PLOS ONE in 2010. The cerebellum fine-tunes movement, and much of its surface layer works through inhibition, one cell quieting another. Small interneurons there send calming signals to the large output cells, to each other, and perhaps to other partners as well.

The team counted and measured these connections in fine detail, giving a firm map of where the calming contacts sit and how many there are. Counts like this are the ground truth that models of the cerebellum must match. They also help researchers spot what changes in diseases that disturb balance and coordination.
plos-pone-0012219:
Antonio Fasanella, Silvia Scasciamacchia, Giuliano Garofolo, and co-authors tested whether house flies can spread anthrax, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Anthrax spores survive for decades in soil, and past work suggested insects help carry them to animals and people during outbreaks. The common house fly feeds and walks on everything, making it a prime suspect as a living ferry for spores.

Their evaluation checks how well flies pick up, carry, and deposit the anthrax bacterium. Knowing the fly's true role decides whether outbreak response should include insect control or focus elsewhere. In farming regions where anthrax still strikes herds, that judgment protects both livelihoods and lives.
plos-pone-0012319:
Amber Carmon, Michael Guertin, Olga Grushko, and co-authors took apart mutations in one of the largest fly genes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The dumpy gene sprawls across seventy-eight coding segments and builds a huge protein of the matrix that surrounds cells, studded with repeating modules. Forty-five known mutations in this one gene offer a rare chance to connect each change in the DNA to a change in the animal.

Their molecular analysis maps where those mutations fall and what they do to the giant protein. Genes this size are hard to study whole, yet they matter: the human counterparts of such matrix proteins underlie many tissue diseases. The fly work shows how to read them.
plos-pone-0012419:
Mary Ann Comunale, Lucy Rodemich-Betesh, Julie Hafner and colleagues studied sugar tags on a blood protein as a liver cancer sign, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Their earlier work showed that proteins gain extra fucose sugar tags as liver cancer develops. One tagged protein, alpha-1-antitrypsin, stood out, and the team checked one specific linkage of that sugar.

That linkage pattern marked patients with liver cirrhosis and cancer in a distinctive way. Blood tests for liver cancer are weak today, and many cases are found late. A sugar-based marker could join the short list of tools for catching liver cancer earlier, when treatment works far better.
plos-pone-0012519:
Laura Bonifacio and Michael Jarstfer profiled tiny RNAs in aging human skin cells, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Cells grown in the lab divide only so many times before senescence stops them, a guard against cancer that also models aging. Adding telomerase, the chromosome-end extender, lets cells bypass that stop, and extended culture alone also leaves marks.

The team compared microRNA profiles across young, senescent, long-cultured, and telomerase-rescued fibroblasts. Each state carried a distinct small-RNA fingerprint. Those fingerprints help separate true aging signals from mere time in a dish, a confusion that has misled aging research before.
plos-pone-0012619:
Quah-Smith, Sachdev, Wen and co-authors used brain scans to test laser acupuncture. In this method, a low laser beam replaces needles at set points on the body. It is used more and more for mental health problems, yet proof of a real brain effect was thin.

Their 2010 study scanned healthy volunteers while laser points linked to mood were stimulated. The scans showed patterns of brain activity that could make the treatment plausible, or fail to. Either way, imaging gives acupuncture claims a fair, measurable test. The work shows how old therapies can be checked with new tools.
plos-pone-0012719:
Wodarczyk, Distefano, Rowe and co-authors showed two kidney disease proteins working as a pair. Faults in the PKD1 gene cause the most common inherited kidney disease, in which cysts slowly wreck the kidneys. Its protein, polycystin-1, ends in a tail that earlier work linked to cell death control.

Their 2010 study found nephrocystin-1 joining polycystin-1 through a short matching motif. The pair then shapes how cells answer death signals. Two disease proteins acting together suggests their illnesses may share one pathway worth targeting.  Both genes were already tied to cystic kidney disorders in families.
pmc-3750319:
Hoesel and Schmid review the complexity of NF-kB signalling in inflammation and cancer. NF-kB is a family of transcription factors, proteins that switch genes on. It has an essential role in inflammation and in the innate immune system, the body's first defence line.

NF-kB is also increasingly recognised as a key player across many steps, from cancer initiation to progression. During those processes it cooperates with multiple other pathways, making its effects context-dependent. The review explains why a promising drug target has proven so hard to tame safely.  Combination therapy ideas in the review stem directly from those pathway interactions described.
pmc-4696819:
Ritz, Baty, Streibig, and their colleagues wrote in 2015 on dose-response analysis using R. Dose-response work asks how an effect grows with dose, a core question in drug and toxicology studies. General commercial software can do it, but non-standard output often needs awkward manual programming.

The authors present the drc extension package for the R environment. It supplies ready models and outputs tailored to dose-response data. That saves time and cuts errors for routine and special cases alike. Free, focused tools help smaller labs run the same quality of analysis as large institutes.
pmc-5395719:
Chalmers, Connelly, Fabrizio, and their colleagues analyzed tumor mutational burden in 2017 across a huge set of human cancer genomes. Tumors that carry many mutations tend to respond better to immune checkpoint drugs, so that mutation load serves as a biomarker. It predicted response to such immunotherapy better than some standard measures.

By studying a very large collection of cancer genomes, the team revealed the landscape of mutational burden across cancer types. Some cancers carry many mutations, others very few, and burden varies within types too. Mutations create new antigens that the immune system can recognize, which explains the link to drug response. The landscape helps oncologists judge who may benefit from checkpoint blockade.
pmc-5735219:
The NCD Risk Factor Collaboration published this pooled analysis of body weight trends in 2017. Being underweight or obese in youth harms health across the whole life course. The team combined thousands of surveys that measured height and weight directly.

The data cover children, teens, and adults in most countries from the mid nineteen seventies to 2016. Results show obesity rising in nearly every region while underweight fell more slowly. The sheer scale makes this a standard source for global weight trends. Governments and health agencies use it to set targets and judge whether policies are working.
pmc-6193719:
Christian Sticht, Carolina De La Torre, Asma Parveen, and coauthors described the miRWalk resource in 2018. MicroRNAs control genes by binding to matching sites on their messages. Guessing those sites well is key to understanding microRNA action.

miRWalk predicts binding sites for genes of humans and several animals and also lists sites proven in experiments. Its core predictor learns from known pairs using a random forest method. A simple web interface serves users who do not code. Researchers start here when a gene change hints that a microRNA might be involved.
pmc-7904519:
Michael Weller and colleagues issued updated guidelines in 2020 on diagnosing and treating diffuse gliomas, a group of brain tumors that grow into surrounding tissue. The European Association for Neuro-Oncology produced the guidance after major changes in how these tumors are classified. Large clinical trials had also recently reported mature results that changed what good care looks like.

The guidelines walk through modern diagnosis, which now leans heavily on molecular features of the tumor, not just its look under a microscope. They then lay out treatment paths for adult patients at each stage. Doctors across Europe and beyond use this document to keep care consistent with the best current evidence.
pmc-7931819:
Petr Danecek and colleagues looked back in 2021 on twelve years of SAMtools and BCFtools, two program suites used to handle DNA sequencing data. The tools manage the standard file formats of the field, converting, sorting, and querying the huge files that sequencing machines produce. They also call genetic variants and analyze their effects.

The article describes what the suites do, how they grew from their first versions, and the standards they helped establish. Almost every genome study of the past decade has passed its data through these programs at some point. The retrospective doubles as a short history of how high throughput sequencing became routine science.
pmc-8866119:
Yunlong Cao and co-authors reported in 2021 that the Omicron variant of SARS-CoV-2 could escape most of the neutralizing antibodies then known. Omicron carried an unusual cluster of changes in its receptor binding domain, the spike region that antibodies target most.
