The team set out at once to learn how those changes affected antibody defenses.

Using a high throughput screening method that tests many antibody interactions at speed, they mapped which antibodies kept working and which failed. Most existing antibodies lost their grip on the variant, while a few broader ones held. Coming within weeks of Omicron's emergence, the results warned that many antibody medicines would need replacing, and that vaccine strategies had to account for this escape.
plos-pone-0359719:
Qing Cui and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on intensive care. It is a retrospective cohort study using the MIMIC-IV database of critical care records. The authors examine early arterial oxygen tension after a line is inserted, and whether it is associated with documented acute thrombosis, blood clots in the upper body or central veins.

Critically ill adults often receive deep lines in the neck or chest, and clots are a known hazard of those lines. An early oxygen reading that flags clot risk would be a cheap warning sign. Intensive care teams are the readers who would weigh this association before changing monitoring practice.
plos-pone-0359419: Li and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on tiny blood vessels in people with chronic kidney disease. The patients were not on dialysis. Looking at the nailfold under a microscope shows the smallest vessels clearly. The team checked which of those vessel signs track with how badly the kidneys fail. A painless peek at the nailfold could one day flag kidney decline early.
plos-pone-0359619: Abrha and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on children recovering from severe malnutrition in Tigray, Northern Ethiopia. The children, aged six to fifty-nine months, were treated in outpatient programs in Adet Woreda. The team measured how long recovery took and what predicted it. Their records-based design looked back at past cases. Knowing what slows recovery helps clinics save more children with the same supplies.
plos-pone-0351819: Vasilikos and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on making a brain covering tissue stronger with light. They used riboflavin, a vitamin, plus UVA light to crosslink collagen in cow dura mater taken from the body. The title reports a controlled, dose-based rise in the tissue's fine-scale strength. Stronger repair tissue could help surgeons patch the membrane that wraps the brain.
plos-pone-0359319: Carvelli and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on what one missing enzyme does to tissue in adult male mice. Without it, guard cells and lining cells in the epididymis, a tube in the male reproductive tract, showed damage under fine-scale viewing. The work links a rare disease enzyme to fertility-related tissue.

europmc-pmc8866119: This 2022 research paper covers omicron escapes the majority of existing SARS-CoV-2 neutralizing antibodies (defense proteins). The SARS-CoV-2 b-1-1-529 variant contains 15 mutations of the receptor (docking point on a cell)-binding domain. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc7295519: Doctors and scientists took on global, local, and national counts of the people at raised risk of severe COVID-19 due to underlying health conditions in this 2020 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Better ways to spot trouble early give doctors a head start on treatment.
europmc-pmc6988219: A fresh look at identifying serious state of complex diseases by single-sample kullback-leibler divergence arrived with this 2020 research paper. Developing effective plans for signaling (cell-to-cell messaging) the pre-disease state of complex diseases, a state with high susceptibility before. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc7170819: Doctors and scientists took on tumor growth and angiogenesis (new blood vessel growth) in adult brain tumor: glioblastoma (an aggressive brain cancer) in this 2020 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc7261819: A fresh look at deqms: a method for accurate variance estimation in differential protein expression (gene activity) analysis arrived with this 2020 research paper. Measured proteomics by mass spectrometry is widely used in biomarker (a body signal that can be measured) research and basic. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
much-ado-about-nothing-pg1519: The famous war of wit between Beatrice and Benedick fills this edition of Shakespeare's sunniest comedy, as friends trick the two sworn singles into love. Meanwhile the gentle Hero is slandered and seemingly lost, until Dogberry's bumbling watch saves the day. Eavesdropping, masked balls, and joy from first line to last.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum: Volume nineteen: the legend of Frederick, how Europe remembered its most famous king. Carlyle traces the making of a myth with his usual force. The vast work reflects on its hero's place in history. Carlyle's Frederick lived on in the German imagination he helped shape.
russia-in-1919: Arthur Ransome, later of Swallows and Amazons, went to Russia in 1919 and wrote what he saw: Lenin, Trotsky, and a land in upheaval. His kind view of the Reds caused a storm at home. A vivid, disputed eyewitness record.
letters-to-dead-authors-pg3319: Andrew Lang's Letters to Dead Authors: epistles to the great. The scholar writes to Homer and Jane Austen. Charming and learned. A bibliophile's delight, lang writes to Homer and Austen, charming and learned, a bibliophile's delight.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-19: The nineteenth volume rounds out the long series of essays. Montaigne's final thoughts on life and death close the set with grace. The circle of self-knowledge is complete at last. A lasting monument of French letters.
plos-pone-0348919:
Sydney P Harned leads a team of five testing how well fish genetics can guide flounder management, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Southern flounder, a prized flatfish, is declining along the southeastern United States coast. Managers need to know whether local groups are separate stocks, and earlier snapshots may mislead. The team sequenced young flounder from estuaries in North Carolina and Texas across a decade, 2014 to 2023, using a genome sampling technique that reads many scattered markers.

Fish from the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic differed clearly and consistently, supporting management as distinct stocks. Inside each region, though, genetic differences between nearby estuaries appeared and vanished from year to year, likely as shifting larval drift and uneven recruitment reshuffled each year's youngsters. The lesson is methodological as much as biological: one season's sample can paint structure that the next season erases.
plos-pone-0336819:
Benjamin Schiek published a study on funding farm research in stages, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Agricultural research for development often proceeds step by step, from lab promise to field trials to wider release. Schiek treated each stage as an option: funders may continue, wait, or stop as evidence grows.

Using real option valuation, a tool borrowed from finance, Schiek priced that freedom to change course. The framework tells funders when early results justify doubling down and when a project should be paused or dropped. Development money is limited, so valuing the option to stop is as important as valuing success. The approach brings discipline to choices often made on hope or habit.
plos-pone-0356919:
Haoyu Wang led a team of seven authors studying bacteria-killing viruses on surfaces, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. These viruses, called phages, must move across a surface to reach the bacteria they kill. The team asked how the surface's shape and texture change that movement, and with it the phages' killing power.

Wang's group showed that surface form does modulate phage mobility, and that potency shifts with it. Designers of phage therapies and antibacterial coatings can use that physics: a surface that helps phages spread may clear bacteria faster. As drug-resistant infections grow, phage tools are drawing fresh interest. This study adds a practical design rule for making them work outside a liquid test tube.
plos-pone-0358219:
Tyler Weide and three colleagues compared groups of sperm by their energy organelles, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Not all sperm in a sample are alike. The team sorted sperm by how many mitochondria each carries, the tiny structures that power the cell, and then compared the nuclear genes in each group.

Weide's group found that the groups differ in their nuclear allele frequencies, the mix of gene variants they carry. That link between energy supply and nuclear makeup hints at hidden sorting in the race to fertilize. Fertility science cares because sperm quality checks now rely on crude measures. A deeper trait like this could refine how samples are judged in clinics and livestock breeding.
plos-pone-0357919:
Juan Carlos Suárez, Amara Tatiana Contreras, and Idupulapati M. Rao published a 2026 plant study in PLOS ONE on tepary bean, a hardy legume, grown under the acidic soils and heat of the Colombian Amazon. They wanted a fair score for how well different bean lines keep photosynthesizing when light, heat, and water stress damage the process. The team grew several hundred accessions in fields and screenhouses, under watered and droughted conditions, and measured their leaves at dawn and midday.

Their stress tolerance index split the collection into five adaptation groups, from highly adapted to very poorly adapted, with most lines in the weaker half. Three accessions stood out, pairing top index scores with thick, chlorophyll-rich leaves and strong photosynthetic efficiency under stress. Those three are nominated as parents for breeding climate-resilient beans for the western Amazon, pending yield trials to confirm their farm value.
plos-pone-0357019:
Hoan Manh Vu and colleagues published a 2026 surgical study in PLOS ONE on a rare pancreatic tumor in children, the solid pseudopapillary neoplasm. Surgeons must clear the tumor while sparing as much working pancreas as they can. The team reviewed every child operated on for this tumor at a tertiary hospital over four years, tracking tumor position, operation, complications, and later function.

Just over thirty children were treated, mostly girls around eleven, usually presenting with abdominal pain. Tumors sat in the head of the pancreas in just under half, and tissue-sparing operations were used in nearly three in five cases. Early complications clustered in head tumors, including one severe leak needing reoperation, but no child died. One recurrence followed a margin-positive sparing operation and was cured by fuller surgery. No child developed lasting hormone problems, and temporary digestive trouble always resolved. A selective tissue-sparing strategy is backed.
plos-pone-0357819:
Lauma Spriņģe and coauthors published a 2026 cross-sectional study in PLOS ONE on how well women in Latvia follow the national cervical cancer screening program, which invites screening every three years. Both screening too rarely and too often can cause harm, so the team surveyed nearly thirteen hundred women aged twenty-five to seventy about their screening history, health, habits, and program knowledge.

One pattern dominated: women who did not know the program's recommended interval were far more likely to be overscreened, underscreened, or unable to recall their screening history at all. Overscreening also clustered among women recruited through a colposcopy clinic, where follow-up care blurs into extra screening. Other health behaviors and background factors mattered less than simple awareness of the rules. Teaching women the right interval, and why more is not always better, they argue, is the cheapest fix for both kinds of non-compliance.
plos-pone-0356619:
Fumitaka Yanase and colleagues published a 2026 randomized trial in PLOS ONE comparing two drip fluids given during major abdominal surgery. Anesthesiologists routinely use compound sodium lactate, but a bicarbonate-buffered fluid avoids adding lactate and might suit high-risk patients better. Fifty adults having elective major abdominal surgery were randomized to one fluid or the other; the main measure was an acid-base number at skin closure.

The trial was designed to show the bicarbonate fluid was not worse by more than a preset margin. It could not: the confidence range for the difference dipped just below that margin in both analyses, so non-inferiority went unproven. One secondary signal favored bicarbonate, with lower blood lactate at surgery's end, but acidity measures did not differ. The result is reported plainly as inconclusive on the main question, in a small trial, with the lactate finding exploratory.
plos-pone-0356719:
Vadim A Bakalin and fellow botanists revise a small genus of liverworts, tiny leafy plants of damp forests, across eastern Indochina. Their 2026 review sorts out six species in the region using both plant form and gene data gathered from many field sites. One species described as new comes from a high plateau in Vietnam's Central Highlands, while an old record from Thailand turned out to rest on a wrong identification.

Two other species were found in Cambodia for the first time, and the region's most common member proved widespread along Vietnam's mountain spine. Gene results also moved two species into a different subgroup than books had claimed. Bakalin and colleagues note the genus never showed its reproductive stage in the region, hinting at strong sensitivity to forest damage.
plos-pone-0346219:
Yasin Arafat and colleagues redesign a plasma jet that pulls nitrogen from air, aiming to cut the heavy energy cost of making fertilizer feedstock this way. Plasma methods could fix nitrogen locally without giant factories, but energy bills have blocked them. Their design swaps the usual water-based ground contact for a fixed grounded electrode and tunes gas mix and flow, checking the plasma's glow to confirm its state.

The fixed-ground version more than doubled output rate and cut energy cost to well under half of the water-ground version in matched runs. Output faded and costs shifted with longer treatment times in both setups. Arafat and colleagues present the electrode change as a concrete step toward plasma nitrogen fixing that farms could one day afford.
plos-pone-0354919:
Bahia Abdallah, Abir Abdel Rahman, Safoura Zangiabadi, and Hala Tamim studied 398 Syrian refugee parents who resettled in Ontario, Canada after 2015 and reported good physical health. Their 2026 cross-sectional study measured depression, anxiety, stress, and post-traumatic stress with standard scales, then compared the scores against how well each family functioned day to day.

Struggling family functioning tracked closely with higher anxiety, stress, and post-traumatic stress, though not with depression. Poorer parents also carried heavier depression, anxiety, and stress. Fathers showed a slight trend toward worse anxiety than mothers. The findings suggest refugee support programs should treat the family's daily functioning and finances as part of mental health care, not as separate problems.
plos-pone-0357119:
Di Tang and colleagues present a protocol, published in 2026, for a twelve-week randomized trial. It asks whether exercise training improves performance in competitive first-person shooter gaming. It also asks which kind of training works better. The planned study will assign 195 gamers aged eighteen to twenty-nine to one of three groups. They are high-intensity interval training, steady moderate training, and a control group, with three sessions weekly.

The main measure is flicking capacity, the snap-aiming skill at the heart of shooter play. Other gaming metrics back it up. So do psychological skills, body composition, and physical fitness. All are rechecked four weeks after training ends, to see whether gains persist. Esports science has mostly tested single workouts. A three-month, three-arm trial would give players and coaches their first durable training guidance.
plos-pone-0345819:
Donna L Schuman and colleagues built and pilot-tested VET-SAVR, a virtual reality simulation. It trains people to spot suicide risk during home visits to rural veterans. This group has elevated suicide rates and thin access to specialists. Their 2026 feasibility study put thirty people through the headset scenario. They were nursing and social work students, health professionals, and rural community members. The scenario teaches risk recognition and counseling on securing lethal means.

Engagement ran high, the scene felt real, and nausea stayed low. Participants reliably recalled the loud cues, firearms and alcohol. They missed quieter ones like isolation. Most judged the simulation authentic. They asked for better navigation and interaction. The team calls it a feasible prototype needing polish before efficacy trials.
plos-pone-0356419:
Anton Björnqvist and four colleagues test whether strategy mapping software can help healthcare staff evaluate their own crisis management, in this 2026 Swedish case study. Fifteen healthcare professionals worked through a four-step workshop series, using the software to lay out causes, effects, and priorities from their crisis experience. The process produced ten recommendations aimed at the risks the group judged most central.

About a year later, the researchers interviewed ten participants about what had stuck. The evaluation was judged impactful, and participants still valued the process, especially rating and ranking the recommendations together. One lesson was that facilitators may need a stronger hand in sharpening recommendations so they stay clear and actionable. The authors offer the approach as a workable template for organizations that want frontline staff, not just managers, to draw the lessons from a crisis.
plos-pone-0355719:
Zhiyuan Mao and co-authors turned fine mine tailings, a powdery waste, into the main ingredient of a water-blocking barrier material. Cement-bentonite walls resist chemical attack poorly, and earlier tailing mixes used tailings only as minor filler. Their 2026 recipe blends full tailings with cement, bentonite clay, and sodium silicate, tuned by single-factor tests.

Raw tailings leaked water roughly a thousand times faster than the modified mixes. Adding cement at fixed clay content raised strength greatly, though it let slightly more water through. Adding clay at fixed cement steadily sealed the material tighter. Microscope scans tied performance to pore structure. Mao and colleagues present the mix for dam and waste-site sealing jobs.
plos-pone-0354519:
Hanh Truong and co-authors make in 2026 a light activated material meant to fight rice blast, a fungus that devastates rice. The material joins a common white pigment with copper in two chemical states, made by a precipitation route. Under visible light from lamps, the copper cycle helps produce aggressive oxygen based particles that stress the fungus.

The version with the most copper blocked fungal growth most strongly after ten days, well above versions with less copper. Light tests confirmed the material absorbed more visible light than the plain pigment. The authors say field value and safety for nature still need checking before farm use.
plos-pone-0354819:
Minyeong Cho and colleagues compare in 2026 three forms of a receptor that guides immune cells toward lymph organs and can aid cancer spread. The forms differ at one end and arise from how the gene message is cut and rejoined. The team cloned each form and tested where it sits in the cell, how it signals, and how forms interact when present together.

One form reached the cell surface well and signalled strongly to both known guide chemicals. A second form barely reached the surface and gave weaker, narrower signals. The third never signalled, bound tightly to the first, and dragged it inside the cell, cutting its responses. Breast cancer cells carrying both forms failed to migrate toward the guides.
plos-pone-0354619:
Zewudu Mulatie led a team of eight authors on this 2026 systematic review of warning flags from automated blood analyzers. These machines flag odd cell patterns that can signal blood cancers such as leukemia or lymphoma. The reviewers pooled accuracy studies from several databases and graded their quality with a standard tool.

Across the pooled studies, the flags worked well as a first screen for blood cancers. Results varied, though, because machines, flag types, and comparison tests differed between labs. Mulatie sees the flags as most valuable where budgets are tight and a fast, cheap early warning matters most.
plos-pone-0355219:
Correction notice: Zhonghan Wu and seven colleagues published this 2026 correction in PLOS One. It fixes parts of their earlier study of a wrist-assisted nail implant for hip fractures in obese patients with weak bones. It is not a new study. The notice replaces two methods sections and the first three tables, whose statistics were wrong.

The corrected text describes a backward-looking cohort at a hospital in Anhui, China, covering patients treated in 2022 and 2023, with a year of follow-up checks. Five hundred patients appear in the corrected tables, split evenly between the new implant and a comparison group. Readers should use these values, not the originals.
plos-pone-0354719:
Xiuli Cheng and five colleagues published this 2026 mouse study asking whether glutamate, a common food and signaling chemical, worsens artery clogging. Mice bred to develop atherosclerosis ate normal or fatty diets, with or without added glutamate, for three months. Plaques were stained and measured, and protein profiles hunted for molecules that changed with the combination.

Glutamate alone caused almost no plaque, but paired with a rich fatty diet it enlarged lesions and raised three proteins. Cheng notes blood glutamate itself did not rise, so changes in blood fats may also share the blame.
plos-pone-0354019:
Adegboyega and colleagues, in a 2026 hospital study in Ilesa, southwestern Nigeria, look at how family life shapes the care of small children with malaria. Malaria still harms many children under five, and late or wrong first steps raise the risk of a bad outcome. Family support, income, and how well a family functions may all steer those first steps.

About three hundred fifty child and caregiver pairs took part. Most caregivers reported strong family support and a well-functioning family, though more than half lived below the study's poverty line. Even so, fewer than half sought care in the way the team judged appropriate. Caregivers from poorer families had about two and a half times the odds of poor care-seeking. Those from families that functioned poorly had about four times the odds. The authors argue that malaria programs should strengthen families and counsel caregivers, not just hand out medicine.
plos-pone-0353519:
Bogale and colleagues, in a 2026 study, report lessons from an effort to strengthen primary health care across Ethiopia. The national Health Extension Program sends community health workers into remote areas, and an optimization project tested new delivery strategies in fourteen districts. Researchers were embedded with the teams, so strategies could be adapted to local conditions while keeping their core intact.

Adaptations were tracked as they happened, and fidelity to the plan's core was monitored across two and a half years. The authors report that adapting strategies to place and culture went together with better coverage of mother and child services. Referral links between clinics strengthened through networks of care, and services were reshaped for pastoralist communities that move with their herds. The paper's wider point is about balance: programs should bend to fit local life without bending so far that the active ingredient is lost.
plos-pone-0354119:
Ying-Ai Cui and three colleagues surveyed unvaccinated medical students in China about the HPV vaccine, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The vaccine prevents cancers caused by human papillomavirus, yet uptake among Chinese students stays low. More than thirty-five hundred students at Guangdong Medical University answered questions on hesitancy and health beliefs in the summer of 2024.

Nearly three quarters said they intended to be vaccinated. Men were far less willing than women, while students who heard about the vaccine from doctors were more willing. Believing vaccination necessary, important, and beneficial all raised intention. The authors suggest clinician-led teaching in the curriculum and support aimed at male students, whom current services barely reach.
plos-pone-0352319:
Brandyn Churchill, Xiaoxue Gao, and Rong Rong ran a vaccine information experiment during the 2024 election season, reported in PLOS ONE in 2026. They recruited nearly three hundred Democrats and a similar number of Republicans in the United States. Participants first estimated COVID-19 infection rates, severity, and vaccination levels, then some learned the true figures and reported whether they now intended to get vaccinated.

Both camps overestimated how common and severe infections were, and how many people were vaccinated — and neither side knew its own party's experience best. The striking result: people who learned they had underestimated the other party's vaccination rate became more willing to vaccinate themselves. Rivalry, it seems, can be turned toward health.
plos-pone-0353119:
Zouzoulas and colleagues laid out a trial plan in 2026 for early, mild cell changes on the cervix. Most such changes clear on their own, so standard care is watching and waiting. The trial tests whether a plant-based supplement that supports immunity helps more changes clear within six months.

Patients with newly confirmed mild changes will be assigned by chance to supplement or watchful waiting alone. Clearance rates will then be compared between the two groups. People with any past cervical changes or pelvic cancer are excluded. If the supplement helps, some patients could avoid long anxious monitoring, though results must come before any such claim is made.
plos-pone-0334819:
Parany and colleagues studied black rat genetics in a plague area of Madagascar in a 2026 paper. Rats carry the plague germ in the highlands, where the disease still returns. Nearly five hundred rats from six villages were sampled indoors and outdoors across two years and tested at many gene markers.

Village groups looked broadly similar, while outdoor rats carried more variety and mixed more freely. Overall separation between groups stayed low, meaning rats move widely and can quickly refill areas after culling. Killing rats alone is thus unlikely to hold, the authors argue. Pairing flea control inside homes with steps that cut contact between people and rats fits the biology better.
plos-pone-0351119:
Xu and colleagues measured airway stiffness in scarred lungs with a light-based probe in a 2026 study. Lung scarring stiffens airways, but standard tests measure the whole lung at once. A thin probe passed into the airways recorded how airway area changed as pressure rose, in healthy volunteers and patients with scarring.

Deeper airway branches in patients tended to show lower stretch than in healthy people. One branch's stretch tracked closely with standard breathing test results. Local stiffness measures could one day spot scarring earlier or follow treatment branch by branch. The small group size makes this a proof of method rather than a clinical rule.
plos-pone-0352119:
Abdi, Bayat, and Mowla studied two tiny gene regulators in the deadliest brain tumor in a 2026 paper. Across ten public data sets, one regulator ran high in tumors while the other ran low, compared with healthy brain. Cell experiments confirmed the same opposing pattern in two tumor cell lines.

Raising the low regulator lowered the high one and raised several of its known target genes. Tumor cell behavior shifted as well, including more cell death. The authors are careful: the link looks functional, not a proven direct binding. Still, restoring the low regulator could be a lever worth testing against a cancer with very few options.
plos-pone-0353219:
Yuhao Wang, Junjie Huang, and Qiang Zhang present this 2026 PLOS One paper on elevator repair. They teach a small language model to diagnose faults and guide upkeep before breakdowns. General models struggle in this niche. They invent answers, lack trade knowledge, and cannot read raw sensor numbers. The team fine-tuned a compact model with step-by-step examples written in varied user styles. They also turned sensor readings into text the model could reason over.

The tuned model gave diagnostic answers far better than a leading general model. Its inner patterns also sorted alarm types well. It predicted vibration levels with skill too. The authors argue that for narrow trade jobs, dense domain training beats raw model size. Small tuned models, they say, offer a cheaper path to automated upkeep advice.
plos-pone-0348719:
Luhang Yu and three co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One deep learning paper on lung tumors. It outlines tumors in ordinary two-dimensional CT slices. Fuzzy borders and odd shapes make that task hard. Their system adds two ideas to a standard backbone. One module treats the tumor edge as uncertain. It samples around a likely boundary. The other nudges outlines toward smooth, plausible shapes, using rules on curvature and compactness.

On two lung cancer datasets, the system beat classic models and mainstream transformer tools on overlap scores. Its boundaries sat much closer to expert outlines than the backbone's alone. The authors argue that handling doubt and shape openly makes tumor maps more trustworthy. Such maps could aid diagnosis and treatment checks. The method needs no extra annotations from experts.
plos-pone-0352019:
Luiz Pimenta and three colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One laboratory comparison of toothbrush types on denture teeth. Bioelectric brushes use a mild current meant to loosen plaque with gentler scrubbing, but their effect on denture wear was unknown. Thirty-six acrylic denture teeth were machine-brushed for the equivalent of about two years of home cleaning, with a manual brush, the bioelectric brush switched off, or the same brush switched on.

Manual and switched-off brushing roughened the acrylic noticeably, while the switched-on brush caused a smaller, statistically insignificant change and left visibly shallower scratches. No group lost measurable weight. Within the limits of a bench model, the authors conclude the active bioelectric brush is kinder to denture surfaces, pending confirmation in real mouths.
plos-pone-0352419:
Kyle Messick and seven co-authors surveyed users of generative artificial intelligence in 2026 about dishonest uses of the technology. The survey covered everything from cheating on schoolwork to misleading people online. Earlier research usually looked at one setting at a time. This study asked whether bad behaviour in one area of life carries into others, and what drives it.

People who used AI unethically in one domain tended to do so in others, and most knew their behaviour was wrong. Misuse was linked with pressure to get results, time pressure, and a feeling that everyone does it and nobody is punished. A wish for social media fame and narcissistic traits also played a part, while self-esteem and loneliness showed no link, which helps target future prevention efforts.
plos-pone-0351319:
Sowmya Pujari and colleagues interviewed twenty mothers from the Koraga tribe of southern Karnataka, India, about how they understand health and feed their young children. The Koraga face deep poverty and poor access to care, and their children carry high rates of undernutrition. Book knowledge of malnutrition rarely explains what mothers actually see and do, so the team listened at length, in the mothers' own languages.

Five themes came out of the conversations, covering changing ideas of health and well-being, beliefs and habits around food, and hygiene and care practices. The accounts show mothers reasoning with what they have, mixing older custom with newer clinic advice. For nutrition programs, the lesson is that messages land only when they fit this local logic, and that mothers here are partners to consult, not empty vessels to fill.
plos-pone-0350919:
Bacteria that shrug off antibiotics thrive where people and farm animals live close together. Amit R Nayak and colleagues lay out a three-year study plan for Nagpur, India, in this 2026 PLOS One protocol, tracking resistant germs across livestock, farm workers, and the farm environment.

Six important bacterial species will be sampled with the seasons, and their drug resistance profiles recorded. The team also plans to study bacteria-killing viruses, called phages, as possible treatments. No results are reported yet. The design follows the One Health idea that human, animal, and environmental health form one connected system.
plos-pone-0351219:
A sudden loss of blood flow to the optic nerve, unrelated to artery inflammation, can permanently narrow vision. Heejin Yoon and colleagues reviewed thirty-eight patients to find which early signs predict whether the visual field recovers, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

About a quarter of the eyes regained a meaningful slice of field within three months. Those eyes started with sharper vision, milder field loss, and lower blood sugar levels. Eye drops sometimes prescribed showed no link to recovery. Starting vision also strongly predicted vision months later. The authors say the baseline picture, taken at the first visit, already carries most of the prognosis.
plos-pone-0348119:
Anthony Train and colleagues traced inhaler prescribing for older adults in Ontario, Canada, from 2017 to 2023. Common puffers release strong warming gases, while dry powder and soft mist types pollute less when they fit the patient. Health records captured three quarters of a million new inhaler starts for people aged sixty five and older, split into before and during pandemic years.

New starts dropped sharply when the pandemic began, then recovered. Puffers stayed dominant, though their share fell from about seventy seven percent to about seventy percent. Powder types gained modest ground. Patterns barely differed by sex, income, or rural home. Greener switching, the authors note, remains slow despite clear climate guidance.
plos-pone-0350219:
Quanwei Shen, Lin Li, and Chenglong Li surveyed six hundred college students in Hubei Province, China, in 2026 about heavy smartphone use. They asked whether self-control lowers phone dependence directly, or through traits such as mental toughness and ease in social life.

Students with stronger self-control reported less phone dependence, as did tougher and more socially at ease students. Social ease carried part of the effect on its own, and toughness and social ease also worked as a chain between self-control and phone habits. The authors suggest colleges build students' confidence in facing problems, not just warn them about screen time.
plos-pone-0349619:
Ahyoung Chang, Seung Gyu Baik, and Junfeng Jiao studied how surroundings shape electric car charging experiences in Travis County, Texas, in 2026. A charger can work perfectly yet still feel poor if the spot is bleak, hard to reach, or short on parking.

More than four thousand user reviews were sorted by language models into themes like operation, access, and parking, then matched to place data. Walkability, greenery, openness, and nearby amenities predicted happy reviews most strongly. Frustrations with access and parking clustered in dense commercial zones. Planners are urged to site chargers as places, not just power points.
plos-pone-0350419:
Mohammed Nasir, Bereket Tessema, and Sura Markos checked how often babies born with a spinal defect also have heart defects at an Ethiopian hospital in 2026. The two conditions share early development pathways, yet African data were thin.

Charts for two hundred sixty-five infants with the spinal defect, all scanned by ultrasound of the heart, were reviewed. About seven in a hundred had a heart defect too. A mother's past miscarriage, overweight, and diabetes each raised the odds. The rate is lower than many might fear, but the linked factors argue for routine heart checks in these newborns.
plos-pone-0326719:
Hannah M Moloney and co-authors valued manta ray watching tourism in the Maldives in 2026. The island nation's rays draw divers from around the world, and putting a money figure on live rays strengthens the case against killing or degrading their habitat.

Surveys of more than one hundred tour operators, plus mined booking data, built the estimate. In 2021 manta tourism generated well over two hundred million dollars in total, split between direct trip spending and wider tourist spending. As the first national valuation, it hands policymakers a concrete counterweight when fishing or development interests press against ray protection.
plos-pone-0350019:
Aniek E M Schouten and co-authors tested a quiet choice that can sway whether a treatment looks worth its cost. Health economists convert quality-of-life survey answers into scores using value sets, and each European country has its own. Their 2026 study re-ran cost analyses from two multinational trials, one on exercise for breast cancer patients and one on a kidney treatment, swapping value sets across countries.

The same answers produced noticeably different scores and health gains depending on which country's values were applied, and the gaps grew when patients reported poor quality of life. Odds that a treatment counted as cost-effective shifted by up to about eleven percentage points. The authors advise testing several value sets in multinational studies instead of trusting just one.
plos-pone-0344519:
Simon Beaufils, Lionel Cavin, and co-authors catalogued the bony fish fossils of the Vaches Noires cliffs in Normandy, a site famous in French paleontology since the seventeen hundreds. The mid-Jurassic fish remains are mostly fragments gathered over years by amateur collectors and kept in public collections. Their 2026 overview gives the first full account of the assemblage, naming each group and estimating body size and feeding level from living look-alikes.

The cliffs preserve a coelacanth, giant filter-feeding and predatory relatives of modern ray-finned fish, armored-scaled forms, and crushing-toothed pycnodonts represented by isolated jaw bones. Small backbones attest to little fish that rarely fossilize whole. The authors compare the assemblage with other Jurassic sites to trace how bony fish diversity and ecology evolved through the period.
plos-pone-0349219:
Bhola Teli and co-authors surveyed first-year engineering students at a Nepali university campus about blood donation, a lifeline that low-income health systems struggle to keep supplied. Their 2026 study questioned one hundred ninety-one students on knowledge, attitudes, and actual giving, then modeled what separates donors from non-donors.

Attitudes were warm: students scored favorably and knew a fair amount. Yet under seventeen percent had ever donated. Women knew more than men, but men were far more likely to have given blood, as were students aged twenty and over. Civil engineering students donated least among the programs. The commonest barriers were having no particular reason and never getting the chance. The authors name this a knowledge-practice gap and suggest campus drives that convert goodwill into appointments.
plos-pone-0350119:
Eugenio Trotta, Paola Palladino, and co-authors pooled the evidence on how memory, feelings, and the teacher relationship shape young children's learning of a second language. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis gathered nineteen studies of primary school pupils, covering more than five thousand children, with sixteen studies feeding the combined statistics.

Working memory correlated positively with language learning, the clearest cognitive signal. Among emotions, anxiety dragged learning down significantly while enjoyment nudged it up slightly. Evidence on the student-teacher relationship was qualitative only, but it consistently suggested that emotional closeness to a teacher buffers children against anxiety during language learning. The authors call for more research on positive emotions and classroom relationships across different school settings.
plos-pone-0349819:
Jun Ho Lee led a study of kidney stones and uric acid in Korea. Uric acid is best known for gout, a joint disease. The team asked if high uric acid, with no gout signs, still tracks with stones. They used checkup records for more than thirty-one thousand adults. Stones were found by scans. The math split men and women and stripped out other risks step by step.

For men, the link held firm at each step. Men in the top uric acid group had more than three times the stone odds of the lowest group. For women, no clear link showed at all. The team calls this a sex-split pattern. They warn that one check in time cannot prove cause.
plos-pone-0348519:
Shravya Chitrapady and colleagues interviewed ten experienced physicians across India about diagnosing acute fevers in tropical settings and about artificial intelligence help. Dengue, scrub typhus, and leptospirosis can look nearly identical at first, yet need different treatment, and lab tools are often limited. The doctors described where their judgment gets stuck.

Interviews were recorded, transcribed, and sorted into themes. Physicians weighed the promise of an AI diagnostic aid against the messy reality of overlapping symptoms and scarce tests. Their views matter because a tool doctors distrust or cannot fit into ward routines will sit unused, however accurate it is. The study feeds those practical concerns into design.
plos-pone-0348819:
Qiufeng Jia and colleagues probed ten leading AI language models for hidden bias in medical decisions. Models can pass open bias tests while still carrying quiet associations between social groups and traits. The team built twenty-four medical test sets spanning gender, race, wealth, health status, religion, and health systems, then measured bias three ways, including word association and comparative decision tasks.

The evaluation covers both commercial systems and open models from several countries. Implicit bias in a tool that drafts advice or triages patients could steer real care unfairly, even when no explicit prejudice appears. A multi-method audit like this shows where the associations live and how strongly they move decisions, giving developers and hospitals concrete targets for correction.
plos-pone-0349019:
Mizanur Rahaman and co-authors made a new electrode material for supercapacitors, devices that charge and discharge far faster than batteries. They grew tiny particles of manganese sulfide inside molybdenum oxide using hot water synthesis. The particles changed the oxide's shape from flat belts to rough fibres, opened wider gaps between its layers, and left a defect-rich surface with much more room for charge to gather.

Electrodes built from the mix stored clearly more charge than the plain oxide in both salt solutions tested. A full two-electrode cell kept about nine tenths of its capacity after a thousand charge cycles. The authors credit the larger surface and wider layers, and they offer the material as a practical step toward faster, longer-lasting energy storage.
plos-pone-0348019:
Lei Xie and Weiran Zhou modelled how city economies, energy use, and environmental quality push on each other over time. They upgraded a standard statistical tool, the vector autoregressive model, with an evolutionary search algorithm to track these moving relationships more faithfully. Their 2026 study draws on urban data to test which forces drive which.

The analysis found two-way influence between energy use and growth, yet energy consumption did not power growth over the long run. Energy's effect on environmental quality swung noticeably over time, while its effect on growth climbed steadily. The authors advise planners to build conservation and emissions cuts into development strategy from the start, rather than treating them as an afterthought.
plos-pone-0346519:
Hanyu Cao and colleagues compared the muscle proteins of a prized Chinese pig breed with a common Western breed to learn why the local pork tastes better. Using advanced mass spectrometry on loin muscle, they catalogued hundreds of proteins differing between Huoshou black pigs and Yorkshire pigs, then cross-checked the standouts with two further methods.

Two hundred sixty-two proteins differed, clustering in metabolism, energy handling, and growth pathways. Five candidate genes emerged linking protein and gene activity to meat quality. The Western breed grows fast and lean; the Chinese breed's chemistry favours flavour and texture. The authors offer molecular targets for breeding programs that want both.
plos-pone-0345719:
Sebastian Ruiz-Blais and colleagues separate singing from slow breathing in this brain study. It appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Toning means holding a sound through one long breath out. Therapists use such vocal work to calm people. No one knew if the voice itself mattered, or only the slow breath it forces.

People with no music training took part. They toned, sang slow songs they knew, and did matched breathing drills. Brain waves and heart rhythm were recorded through each task. The contrasts show which changes belong to making sound. They also show which belong to pacing the breath. If breath alone does the work, therapy can stay simple.
plos-pone-0347919:
Zeyu Zhu studies how the time people take to decide predicts their next move in a cooperation game, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Reanalyzing data from a network public goods experiment, he treats decision time as a sign of inner conflict: people torn between self-interest and the group deliberate longer.

Slow deciders were more likely to flip their choice in the next round. Among defectors, the fast ones were keener to form new social links, while fast cooperators shunned links with defectors more than slow cooperators did. Because thinking time is easy to observe, it could help design interventions that nudge networks toward cooperation without prying into motives.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Late in 1965, the Council renewed the Cyprus force once more. On 17 December, it adopted Resolution 219 without dissent. The Secretary-General's report said the force was still needed on the island. The Cyprus government agreed it should stay past late December.

The text restates the whole chain of earlier Cyprus decisions. The chain starts with Resolution 186 of 1964. It then extends the posting by three months, to 26 March 1966. Short renewals like this turned an emergency mission into a fixture. The island's two peoples stayed split, and no deal was in reach. Each renewal bought quiet, not a cure.

Namibia's fate still hung on talks in 1972. South Africa ruled the land in defiance of the UN. A fresh push for contact had begun that February. The chief had met the sides and sent in word. Resolution 319 passed on 1 August 1972 by fourteen votes to none.

The Council thanked the chief for his work. It restated Namibia's right to rule itself. The land had to stay whole and one. The chief was told to keep up his contacts. He would work with a small Council group. A named aide could join the effort to help him. The aim was stark: let the people choose their fate as free and equal men and women. A progress note was due by 15 November.

Murdered aid workers in West Timor drive Resolution 1319, adopted on 8 September 2000. Two days earlier a militia-led mob had killed three United Nations refugee workers at Atambua, and more attacks followed at Betun. The killings landed during the UN Millennium Summit, where the Secretary-General and several heads of government voiced outrage in the hall.

The Council condemned the killings as an outrageous act against unarmed staff who were helping East Timorese refugees. It demanded that Indonesia disarm and disband the militias in the camps, make the area safe for refugees and aid workers, and bring those responsible to justice. Refugee intimidation, it insisted, had to end so people could choose freely whether to go home.

Resolution 1819, passed on 18 June 2008, keeps the expert team on Liberia's bans in place. The Council had let the ban on Liberian wood lapse by choice. It had ended the ban on rough gems the year before. Liberia had joined the world gem-check scheme and passed a woods law in 2006. Work stayed undone on land rights, on saving wild woods and beasts, and on fair deals for logging firms.

The expert team won a fresh span of work. It would track Liberia's gains and weigh what the last bans still did. The Council stressed that the UN force still counted for safety across the land. The state had to plant its writ in the gem and wood zones most of all.

Resolution 419, adopted on 24 November 1977, follows up an attack on the People's Republic of Benin by foreign mercenaries on 16 January 1977. A Council mission had already looked into the raid, and Benin's representative warned of more threats. Members said hired fighters from abroad were a danger to all states, above all small ones.

The Council backs its earlier Resolution 405, which condemned the attack and all outside meddling in a country's own affairs. It takes note of a report on the damage done and calls on states to share what they know about the mercenaries involved. It notes Benin's wish to see the attackers face due process in court. It also appeals for help to repair the damage and asks the Secretary-General to support Benin and report by 20 September 1978.

Sudan's mission is extended into the referendum countdown in Resolution 1919, adopted on 29 April 2010. Nationwide elections had just been held in April. The Comprehensive Peace Agreement was at a critical stage. The 2011 referenda on South Sudan's future and the popular consultations lay ahead. Localized violence, especially in the south, and Lord's Resistance Army activity threatened civilians.

The Council extends the United Nations Mission in Sudan, UNMIS, until 30 April 2011. UNMIS must be ready to help prepare the 2011 referenda. It must support the Abyei arbitration outcome, north-south border demarcation, and wealth sharing. It must apply a mission-wide strategy to protect civilians, including refugees, displaced people, and returnees. Quarterly Secretary-General reports must detail referendum support plans, post-referendum issues, and planning for the UN presence after the interim period. The Council also asks UNMIS to coordinate with other regional missions against the LRA threat.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 19, adopted on 6 February 1946 at the twenty-third plenary meeting, fixed the pay of the judges of the International Court of Justice. The president and members were each set a yearly salary of 54,000 florins. The president drew a special allowance of 15,000 florins. Extra judges called in for a case were paid by the day, with a daily living allowance.

In resolution 69/19 (2014), the General Assembly follows up its long-running project for a permanent memorial at United Nations Headquarters honoring the victims of slavery and the transatlantic slave trade. The text recalls the annual International Day of Remembrance on 25 March and the educational purpose behind the memorial.

The Assembly notes that the design 'Ark of Return' has been selected and construction is under way. It decides the memorial will sit within the Headquarters campus. It says leftover trust-fund money will support its upkeep. It thanks contributors and urges further voluntary donations. It asks for annual commemorative activities and public-awareness work. It asks for reports on outreach and on the fund at the seventieth session. The memorial was meant to make remembrance a permanent physical presence at the United Nations, not only an annual observance.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Security Council resolution 119 was adopted on 31 October 1956, by 7 votes to 2, with 2 abstentions. It addresses the grave situation created by the military action taken against Egypt in the Suez crisis. Disagreement among its permanent members at two earlier meetings had stopped the Council from carrying out its main responsibility for peace and security. Noting that, it decides to call an emergency special session of the General Assembly. The session is under the 'Uniting for Peace' resolution 377 A (V). The Assembly can then make appropriate recommendations.

A milestone in Afghanistan's recovery, the Emergency Loya Jirga, is welcomed on 26 June 2002. The grand assembly had met from 11 to 19 June under the Bonn Agreement. The Council noted with special satisfaction the large share of women taking part and the presence of all ethnic and religious communities.

The Afghan people are commended, and all groups are urged to work with the new Transitional Authority to finish the Bonn process. The Authority is pressed to fight the poppy crop, advance the welfare of women and children, and provide schooling for girls and boys alike. Far greater aid is also called for, so refugees and displaced Afghans can return home.

A new monitoring team for the Somalia arms embargo is set up on 16 December 2003. The embargo, in place since 1992, kept being broken, most recently tracked by a panel whose work was ending. Peace talks for Somalia were under way in Kenya under regional sponsorship.

The Secretary-General is asked to establish a Monitoring Group of up to four experts, based in Nairobi for six months. Its focus is ongoing embargo violations, including transfers of ammunition, single-use weapons, and small arms. Somali and regional parties, officials, and states are all told to cooperate fully with the group, and any refusal is to be reported through the sanctions committee.

Iraq's assistance mission, UNAMI, is extended for another twelve months on 11 August 2005. The mission had been created in August 2003 and renewed a year later. The national dialogue UNAMI supports is stressed as crucial to Iraq's political stability and unity.

The extension runs twelve months from adoption, and the mandate would be reviewed within that time, or sooner if Iraq's government asked. The United Nations' leading role in helping Iraqis build institutions for representative government is restated. The Secretary-General's August letter on the mission, which informed the decision to keep UNAMI in place, is also noted.

A new United Nations office for Burundi is created on 25 October 2006, as the peacekeeping operation there winds down. Burundi's transition had ended with an elected government. A Comprehensive Ceasefire Agreement with the last rebel group, the Palipehutu-FNL, had been signed in Dar es Salaam in September 2006.

The Secretary-General is asked to establish a United Nations Integrated Office in Burundi, BINUB, to succeed the peacekeeping operation. The office would back peacebuilding, security reform, justice, and development under Burundian ownership, with special attention to women's rights and gender questions. Burundian actors are urged to pursue the remaining reforms and to investigate reported abuses fully.

The Corfu Channel dispute between the United Kingdom and Albania takes a first step on 27 February 1947. Incidents in the channel had brought the two countries before the Council. Before judging the case, the Council wanted the facts established from the evidence available.

A sub-committee of three of its members is appointed to examine all the evidence on the incidents. The sub-committee had to report on the facts by 10 March 1947. It could ask the two governments for more information, and both were told to give it every assistance. The dispute later went to the International Court of Justice, in one of that court's earliest cases.

The long war between Iran and Iraq was ending in 1988, and its cease-fire needed watchers. Resolution 598 of 1987 had demanded that cease-fire. The Secretary-General had now reported on how to put the demand into effect. Resolution 619 was adopted on 9 August 1988.

The Council approved the Secretary-General's report. It set up a United Nations Iran-Iraq Military Observer Group, called UNIIMOG, at once and under its own authority. The group was established for a period of six months, unless the Council decided otherwise. The Secretary-General was told to take the steps needed to put the plan into practice. He also had to keep the Council fully informed of further developments. The observers would watch the cease-fire on the ground while the two countries moved toward a settlement.
un-sc-res-219:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force was renewed at the end of 1965, in a pattern that had become familiar. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 10 December, said the force was still needed on the island. Cyprus's government agreed it should stay beyond 26 December 1965. Resolution 219 was adopted unanimously on 17 December 1965.

The Council reaffirmed its line of Cyprus resolutions, from Resolution 186 of 1964 onward. The force's stationing was extended once again. This time the extension ran for three months, ending on 26 March 1966. The Council also thanked the Secretary-General for his efforts on Cyprus. Short renewals like this one kept the peacekeepers in place through the 1960s. Each one bought a few more months of quiet while a settlement stayed out of reach.
un-sc-res-319:
Namibia diplomacy moved slowly through 1972, and the Council kept it alive. The Secretary-General had reported on his contacts with the parties. On 1 August 1972 the Council thanked him for that work. It restated the Namibian people's right to self-determination and independence. It also restated the territory's unity and wholeness. South Africa still ran Namibia in defiance of the United Nations.

The Secretary-General had to continue his contacts with all concerned. A small group of Council members would work with him. Their aim was to create the conditions for Namibians to choose freely. The text builds on resolution 309 of that February. The effort stalled the next year, but the legal position never moved.
un-sc-res-1319:
Murdered aid workers in West Timor forced the Council's hand on 8 September 2000. A militia-led mob had killed three United Nations refugee staff on 6 September. Attacks in Betun the next day reportedly killed refugees as well. Two UNTAET peacekeepers had also been murdered in East Timor. Indonesia's president wrote on 7 September promising a full inquiry and firm steps against the guilty.

The Council insisted that Indonesia take further steps. The militia had to be disarmed and broken up, law and order restored in West Timor, and safety secured in the refugee camps. Those behind the attacks on international staff had to face justice. Indonesia was called to stop militia raids across the border into East Timor. Its plan to send more troops was noted. UNTAET, for its part, had to answer the militia threat with force. The Secretary-General owed the Council a report within a week.
un-sc-res-1819:
Liberia's expert watchers were renewed on 18 June 2008. The government had made steady progress since January 2006 in rebuilding the country. Timber measures had been dropped after the 2006 forestry reform law, and the diamond measures had ended too. Liberia had joined the Kimberley Process and set up its internal controls. UNMIL still helped the state hold the diamond and timber regions and the borders.

The Council asked the Secretary-General to renew the Panel of Experts on Liberia to 20 December 2008. Its task was to check the remaining sanctions, above all the arms embargo and the asset freeze on listed persons. All states and Liberia's government had to cooperate with the panel. The government was encouraged to apply the Kimberley Process advice and to keep its forest reforms working. UNMIL's help to the government, and the Côte d'Ivoire mission's watch on the shared border, were both reaffirmed.
un-sc-res-419:
Benin's mercenary invaders were pursued through paperwork on 24 November 1977. Mercenaries had attacked Benin on 16 January 1977, flying into Cotonou at dawn. A Council mission had reported on the raid, and a damage assessment now lay in document S/12415. The Council judged such fighters a danger to all states, above all the small.

The Council restated resolution 405 (1977), which had condemned the armed aggression against Benin in the strongest terms. All states were called to work closely together to gather every fact about the mercenaries who took part in the January attack. Benin's wish to see those men face due process of law was noted. States and aid bodies were appealed to for help rebuilding what the raid had damaged. The Secretary-General had to give Benin the help needed and watch over the text's working, reporting back to the Council as required.
un-sc-res-1919:
Sudan moved through the Council as Resolution 1919, adopted on 29 April 2010. National elections had just been held that April, the first in decades. A referendum on southern self-rule was due in January 2011. Local violence inside Southern Sudan kept flaring despite the 2005 peace deal.

The Council extends the United Nations Mission in the Sudan, called UNMIS, until 30 April 2011. The mission should take the lead in helping prepare the referendums, including advice on security. It must build a mission-wide plan to shield civilians and boost its presence where clashes loom. Both sides are told to honor the peace deal in full. Reports come every three months.
un-ga-res-address-to-the-united-nations-:
George W. Bush, president of the United States, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on September 19, 2006. He spoke while the Iraq war, launched by his government in 2003, faced sharp criticism around the world. The yearly general debate gave him a direct line to friend and critic alike.

Bush defended his freedom agenda and said the war on terror served all free states. He spoke to the people of Iraq, Iran, and Syria over the heads of their rulers. He also backed aid, debt relief, and talks on trade. The speech is a clear record of his case, in his own words.
europmc-pmc10019719:
Pak and co-authors test whether AlphaFold can predict how single mutations change a protein's stability and function, in a 2023 study. AlphaFold predicts protein shapes from sequence with striking accuracy. Some had even claimed the protein folding problem was solved. The authors ask a harder question: can the tool sense small changes?

They compare AlphaFold predictions for normal and mutated proteins across known cases. Their checks show where the tool helps and where it stays blind to change. The study gives a sober guide for researchers who want to use AI shapes in mutation work.
europmc-pmc10316519:
Rusch, Layden, and Dugas wrote a 2023 review on how gut microbes may shape thought and memory. The gut holds vast numbers of microbes, with more genes than the human body itself. These microbes talk to the brain through nerves, hormones, and the immune system.

One key path runs through the stress system, which makes the hormone cortisol. The right level of cortisol helps the brain grow and helps learning. Rusch reports that microbes affect this stress system across the whole life span. Stress can also disturb the gut and brain link. Most proof so far comes from animal studies, and human trials are now under way.
europmc-pmc10355019:
Tu and Wang, with the Special Writing Group of China Stroke Surveillance Report, summed up stroke in China in 2021. Stroke has led deaths and disability in China since 2015. A stroke strikes when blood flow to the brain is blocked or a vessel bursts. The report draws on national screening and hospital data.

An estimated 17.8 million adults in China had had a stroke by 2020. About 3.4 million had their first stroke that year, and 2.3 million died that year. Most strokes, at 81.9 percent, came from blocked vessels. High blood pressure touched 24.7 percent of adults, yet just a quarter of cases were well controlled. Hospital care for stroke cost about 58 billion yuan in 2020.
europmc-pmc10356619:
Hickey and colleagues mapped the human gut at single-cell scale in 2023. The gut runs over nine metres and its jobs shift along its length. The team took samples from eight gut sites in nine donors. They used image scans and tests of gene activity in single cell cores.

Cell mixes differed a lot from site to site. Hickey found many subtypes among the surface cells that line the gut. The same cell types grouped into distinct zones, which formed immune niches, or local defence hubs. Gene control patterns hinted at a step-by-step path as cells mature. The team also linked gut disease risk genes to specific cell types.
europmc-pmc10550819:
Zhou led a team in 2023, with the UK Biobank Eye & Vision Consortium, to build a base AI model for eye scans. Most medical AI models learn from labelled scans, which take expert time to mark. Each model also fits just one task. Their model, RETFound, learned from raw scans with no labels at all.

Training used 1.6 million retinal images, the photos of the back of the eye. Zhou then tuned the model for set tasks with a small stock of labelled scans. It beat rival models at spotting eye diseases that threaten sight. It also foretold body-wide ills such as heart failure and heart attack. The shared base cuts the expert marking that clinics must fund.
europmc-pmc11324519:
Camargo and colleagues present a framework that finds mobile genetic elements in sequencing data in this 2024 paper. Mobile elements, such as plasmids and viruses, move genes between microbes. They shape ecology, biotechnology, and public health. Spotting them in vast sequence data is essential but hard.

Their tool, geNomad, blends gene content with a deep neural network to classify sequences. It draws on over 200,000 marker protein profiles to annotate genes and assign viral taxonomy. A statistical model detects proviruses, viral DNA woven into a host genome, with high precision. Benchmark scores reached 77.8 percent for plasmids and 95.3 percent for viruses, substantially beating rival tools. The team processed over 2.7 trillion base pairs and found millions of new viruses and plasmids, shared via public databases.
europmc-pmc1183519:
Grün and colleagues mapped tiny gene regulators in fruit flies in 2005. These regulators are called microRNAs, short bits that curb protein output. Each one binds to matching sites on gene messages. The team used a program named PicTar to predict targets.

Comparisons across seven fly species sharpened the search. On average, each microRNA was linked to about 54 target genes. Some clustered microRNAs seem to act as a team. Grün also compared fly targets with mammal targets. A few control links appear shared, while others seem unique to each group.
europmc-pmc1195719:
Liu and co-authors mapped chemical marks on yeast DNA packaging in 2005. DNA wraps around histone proteins in units called nucleosomes. Small chemical marks on histones affect gene use and repair. Many mark types exist, and their combined patterns were unclear.

A fine-scale chip read 12 mark types on thousands of units. Marks did not occur at random or alone. They fell into roughly two partner groups. One group left a distinct zone near gene start sites. Liu shows packaging marks form patterns, not noise. Those patterns may encode gene control rules.
europmc-pmc1253619:
Molyneux, Hotez, and Fenwick proposed bundled control of neglected tropical diseases in 2005. Seven infections in Africa anchor their plan. Such diseases deepen poverty and carry stigma in rural areas. Past campaigns had already cut several of them sharply.

Treating the seven together would cost about 40 cents per person yearly. Hundreds of millions could gain lasting benefit from that spend. Guinea worm may even face eradication soon, they note. Lymphatic filariasis, river blindness, leprosy, and trachoma had all receded. Molyneux argues joint delivery beats one-disease campaigns for the poor. These infections are ancient, noted in the Bible and other old texts. They have burdened people for ages.
europmc-pmc13324819:
Alexander and the Concise Guide team catalogued G protein-coupled receptors in 2023. The guide is the sixth biennial edition of a pharmacology reference. It summarizes about 1,800 drug targets in compact tables. Roughly 6,000 interactions with about 3,900 ligands are covered.

Receptors in this section form one of six major target classes. Entries stress selective pharmacology where it exists. Links point to the open Guide to Pharmacology database. The printed guide runs almost 500 pages yet condenses the website. Alexander provides a permanent, citable snapshot of receptor knowledge. Other sections cover ion channels, hormone receptors, enzymes, and more. Each edition freezes the fast-moving database at one set date.
europmc-pmc1391919:
Bentley and co-authors sequenced the capsule genes of all 90 pneumococcal serotypes in 2006. The pneumococcus wears a sugar capsule to survive in blood. That capsule also defines vaccine targets and serotypes. Each serotype makes a chemically distinct capsule.

Sequences were related to known sugar structures and typing serum reactions. The full set gives the most complete picture of capsule diversity origins. The complete gene repertoire enables a full analysis of one capsule system. It also lays foundations for molecular serotyping. Bentley lays groundwork for tracking vaccine escape types. It appeared in PLoS Genetics in 2006.
europmc-pmc1457019:
What drives year-to-year swings in Lyme disease risk? Ostfeld and co-authors spent 13 years on that question in 2006, in New York forests where the disease is common. Risk rests on how many young ticks carry the Lyme germ. They weighed weather, deer counts, rodent counts, and acorn crops as drivers.

Deer counts had no power to foretell risk. Rain and warmth had weak effects at best. The best clues were mice and chipmunk counts from the year before, plus acorn crops two years back. Ostfeld concludes that food for tick hosts, and the hosts themselves, set the risk people face.
europmc-pmc1852419: microRNA expression in the prefrontal cortex of individuals with schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder. — a 2005 science paper on tiny RNAs in mental illness. It maps the tiny-RNA signs for labs. The paper is the tiny-RNA study: the notes on brain-ill signs, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc1977719: Phase I trial of temozolomide (CCRG 81045: M&B 39831: NSC 362856). — a 2005 science paper on a temozolomide trial. It runs the Phase I trial. The paper is the trial study: the findings on temozolomide, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2206519: Urine neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin is an early marker of acute kidney injury in critically ill children: a prospective cohort study. — a 2005 science paper on a kidney-injury pee marker. It tests the early marker. The paper is the marker study: the findings on kidney ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2409519: Serum levels of IL-6 and TNF-alpha correlate with clinicopathological features and patient surv — a 2008 science paper on IL-6/TNF in cancer. It correlates the serum levels. The paper is the correlate study: the findings on serum ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2697319: Rheological and physiological consequences of conversion of the maternal spiral arteries for ut — a 2008 science paper on womb-artery flow shifts. It maps the flow shifts for labs. The paper is the flow study: the notes on womb ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2757919: Multiple sclerosis: microRNA expression profiles accurately differentiate patients with relapsi — a 2008 science paper on MS micro-tag sorts. It sorts the MS tags for labs. The paper is the sort study: the notes on MS ills, filed here in full session today twice.
plos-pone-0004919:
Copper is a metal that every cell needs in tiny amounts. Its balance inside cells shifts as they grow old. Christian Scheckhuber and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 on that shift. They tracked copper in ageing cells of the fungus Podospora anserina, a classic ageing model. They also tracked it in ageing human skin cells called fibroblasts.

Their measurements pointed to mitochondria as major players in the change. Mitochondria are the cell's energy producers. The same kind of shift appeared in the human cells, not just the fungus. That parallel suggests some features of cellular ageing are shared across very different forms of life.
plos-pone-0005019:
Lead in city air has fallen for decades. Even so, children need still lower exposure. This potent neurotoxin harms the developing brain. Nicholas Pingitore and colleagues hunted its remaining source. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They used X-ray absorption spectroscopy on urban airborne lead.

The analysis fingered urban soil as the dominant source. Factories and traffic were not the main culprits anymore. Old lead settled in soil keeps rising into the air as dust. The finding points cleanup at the ground beneath cities. It also explains why air lead resists further decline. Soil is a long memory for past pollution.
plos-pone-0005119:
Viruses engineered to kill cancer are called oncolytic viruses. Some replicate only in tumor cells. Their clinical efficacy is still limited by poor infection of the tumor mass. Verónica Lopez and colleagues studied a missing factor in PLOS ONE in 2009. The factor is the tumor's stromal cells. These support cells talk constantly with malignant cells.

Tumor-associated stromal cells play a critical role in the outcome. They can shield the tumor from the viral attack. Beating cancer with viruses means beating its neighborhood too. The study used conditionally replicative adenoviruses. It shows efficacy depends on more than the virus and the cancer cell. Trial designers should measure the stroma's role. Patients might be chosen by stromal features.
plos-pone-0005219:
Melanoma that has spread is hard to treat and lacks reliable blood markers to track it. Tumors shed tiny vesicles called exosomes, which carry proteins from the cells that made them. Logozzi and colleagues measured those vesicles in melanoma patients in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Patients carried high levels of exosomes marked with the proteins CD63 and caveolin-1 in their plasma. Healthy tumor-derived vesicles also play roles in cancer growth, so the signal is biologically plausible. A blood test based on vesicles could track disease without repeated tissue samples.
